activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The yellow first-down line shown on televised American football is computer-drawn; it was first broadcast on ESPN on September 27, 1998, by a company called Sportvision.
story:
The cousin, who was seven and had claimed the good chair before anyone else arrived, pointed at the screen with a pretzel rod. "Why do they paint a yellow line on the grass if they keep moving it every play?"

Morgan looked up from her phone. Her grandfather's den smelled like chili and radiator dust, and the game filled the big television he'd bought after grandma died, as if a bigger screen could fill the room by itself. "They don't paint it," she said. "It's not really there."

He squinted at her. "It's right there."

Camilla, folded into the corner of the couch with her boots still on, said, "Wait, is that true? I've watched football my whole life and I never thought about it."

Morgan hadn't thought about it either until last semester, when Sara-Maude had shown her a video in the library during a free period. At the time Morgan had assumed it was a minor thing, a trick like any other trick, and had gone back to her chemistry homework. Now, with three people waiting and the cousin's pretzel suspended midair, she found she couldn't remember the details cleanly. "It's added by a computer," she said. "For the broadcast. The players can't see it. Only we can."

"That's insane," Camilla said.

The cousin absorbed this with visible suspicion. He leaned toward the screen, then toward the window, where the actual November yard was going grey. "So the players don't know where the line is?"

"They know where it is," Morgan's father said from the kitchen doorway. "They just can't see the yellow part."

"He's seven," Morgan said.

"I'm eight," the cousin said.

Sara-Maude arrived late, shaking rain off her jacket, and dropped onto the arm of the couch. "Are we winning?"

"We're not playing," Camilla said. "We're watching."

"Same thing in this house." Sara-Maude stole a handful of pretzels from the cousin, who retaliated by sitting on her foot.

Morgan kept thinking about the yellow line. She remembered now that Sara-Maude's video had said the first broadcast with it was on ESPN, and the date had stuck with her because it was three days before her own birthday, though years earlier, before she was born. September 27, 1998. She said it out loud to test it. "September 27, 1998. ESPN. That's when the first one went out."

Sara-Maude frowned. "You actually retained that?"

"It invigorated me," Morgan said, and Camilla laughed at her, and she didn't care. "There was a company that did it. Sportvision. They drew the line and the broadcast showed it and after that every game had one."

The cousin had gone quiet, working through something. "So before that," he said slowly, "people watching didn't know where the first down was?"

"They had to guess. Or the announcer told them."

"That's so bad." He seemed genuinely troubled, and Morgan recognized the feeling, the small vertigo of learning that a thing you'd assumed was the world was actually an addition to it. She'd had it once about the stars, when her grandfather, sharpening a pencil at the kitchen table for no reason she ever learned, mentioned that some of them were already gone.

Mr. Oliveira, the neighbour who let himself in through the back door during every home game as though the schedule were his idiosyncrasy and not a habit, appeared with a bowl of his own trail mix. "Who's explaining broadcast graphics to a child?"

"He asked," Morgan said.

"Nobody ever asks the important questions at halftime," Mr. Oliveira said, and settled into the last chair.

On the screen the running back broke a tackle and carried for eleven yards, and the yellow line, which had been at the twenty-six, was suddenly at the thirty-five, and Morgan watched the cousin watch it, checking whether the players looked down at the turf as they crossed it. They didn't. They never did. He turned to her with the expression of someone who had caught the universe in a small lie.

"Okay but who decides where it goes?"

"The referees," her father called. "The line just shows what they decided."

"So it's real and not real at the same time."

Morgan opened her mouth to correct him, then stopped, because he wasn't wrong, and she wasn't sure she could say it better. "Yeah," she said. "Pretty much."

"Football is so weird," the cousin said, and ate the pretzel rod whole.

The extra point went up, wobbling, and the whole room groaned before it sailed through, and Sara-Maude pulled the bowl of trail mix onto her lap like she'd earned it.

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: Need-blind admission means a college decides whom to admit without considering whether the applicant can afford to pay; many US colleges are instead need-aware.
story:
The mailbox at the end of the driveway still had last winter's wasp nest in the corner, a gray paper comma that Emma had never bothered to knock out. She checked the box twice on the first of April, once before the bus and once after, and on the second check there were three envelopes, two thin and one thick. The thin ones were from the state schools, which had said yes back in December. The thick one had a crest on it and a return address she recognized, and she stood in the driveway turning it over so many times that Oscar, who had come around the corner with his bike helmet still buckled, said, "Open it or don't, but decide before my mom texts me for dinner."

She opened it. The first word was Congratulations, and the second paragraph, when she found it under the confetti she hadn't expected, said that financial aid information would follow in a separate letter. "Then it's good," Oscar said. "That's good, right?" Emma said yes, it was good, but she was already doing the arithmetic she had been doing since autumn, which was that the college she most wanted was one of the ones on her list that looked at finances when deciding, and this one, the one in her hand, did not, or claimed not to, and she had spent months not-quite-trusting that claim.

"You keep saying that like it means something," Oscar said, riding slow beside her as she walked. "Need-blind," Emma said. "It means they decide who gets in without looking at whether you can pay." Oscar steered around a storm drain. "And the others look?" "The others look. They're need-aware. So a school that's aware of need can think twice about a kid whose family can't cover it, near the end of the admit pile." She heard how it came out, like a definition recited, and shrugged. "I found it out in January, after I'd already sent everything."

What she didn't say to Oscar, because she hadn't finished saying it to herself, was that in January she had stood in Ms. Müller's classroom after last bell with her list of nine colleges and a highlighter, and Ms. Müller had said nothing at all, only slid the printed aid pages across the desk and let Emma read. Emma had gone home and made two columns in her notebook, the blind ones and the aware ones, and discovered that the schools most likely to admit her were the aware ones, because her grades were the kind that got read generously at places trying to fill a middle of the class, and the schools she loved were the blind ones, which could afford to reject her without ever knowing what she'd have cost them. It was a strange comfort, being rejected blind. It felt clean, like weather.

Hasan had taken the opposite view, the one she kept arguing against and then quietly adopting pieces of. "If they don't know you're poor, they don't know you're poor," he'd said over lunch, crumbling the foil of his sandwich into a ball. "They're deciding on you like you're anybody. That's the fairest thing there is." Emma had said fairness wasn't the same as honesty, and Hasan had said neither of them was blase enough to pretend college admissions were either one, and they'd laughed, but she'd gone on thinking about it for days. Was it better to be judged on paper that showed only her mind, or to be known whole, finances and all, and admitted anyway? The first felt like a reprieve from being her family's tax return. The second felt like being seen. She could not make the two line up, and she had begun to suspect they never would, and that this was allowed.

The follow-up letter came a week later while her mother was at her second shift. Emma took it to the front steps and read it in the long light. The blind college, the one that had congratulated her, offered aid that would leave about eleven thousand dollars a year for her family to cover, which was the gap her mother had named in November, quietly, at the kitchen table, as the number that would require a second job or a loan or both. The state schools, the aware ones, the ones that had known her down to her mother's W-2 before they said yes, had left a smaller gap. Two of them had left almost nothing.

She sat on the steps doing what she had learned to do that year, which was hold two truths side by side without forcing them into a single sentence. The blind school had admitted her without knowing what she'd cost, and that admission was worth something she couldn't price, a kind of respect. The aware school had known everything and said yes anyway, and that was worth something too. If she chose the cheap one, she would owe less and maybe regret the other forever, or maybe not, maybe the regret would calcify into a story she told at parties about the school she almost went to. If she chose the expensive one, she would spend four years watching her mother's hands. Neither was a clean decision. Both were honest ones.

Her mother's car turned in at nine, tired in the way that had its own grammar. Emma stood up with both letters, the fat envelope and the thin one, and held them out. "The one I loved admitted me without asking if we could pay," she said. "The one I could afford asked, and took me anyway." Her mother set down her bag and looked at the envelopes for a long moment, then at Emma. "Which one costs less?" she said. Emma pointed to the thin one, and her mother nodded slowly, and Emma said, "That's what I thought you'd ask," and then, "Can we sit at the table and read them both again, together, before we decide anything?"

activity: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
knowledge_domain: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
fact: Minnesota's Department of Transportation says the zipper merge, using both lanes up to the merge point and then taking turns, can cut a backup's length by as much as 40 percent.
story:
The garage smelled like oil and old hockey gear, and Cole sat in the driver's seat of his mother's sedan with the door open, one foot still on the concrete. Mr. Thompson, the neighbour who had agreed to supervise, folded himself into the passenger seat with a thermos and a clipboard he clearly did not need. "Cones are set up on the street," he said. "You're going to parallel park between them until it stops feeling like surgery."

It felt like surgery for the first forty minutes. Cole backed in too fast, straightened too late, and once mounted the curb so gently that it took him a second to realize he'd done it. Mr. Thompson sipped his coffee and offered commentary in the tone of a golf announcer. "A bold choice, positioning the car partly on the sidewalk." From the driveway, Madelyn and Kristian watched from lawn chairs they had dragged over from her yard, keeping score. Kristian held a notebook in which he claimed to transcribe every mistake for posterity, and he read a few aloud: "Three forty-one p.m., subject kills engine mid-maneuver. Three forty-three, subject curses at a traffic cone."

"The cone deserved it," Cole said through the window. "It moved."

"Cones are stationary," Madelyn said. "It's basically their whole personality."

By late afternoon, something loosened. The tenth attempt, the car slid into the space with a foot to spare on each side, and Cole sat there gripping the wheel, waiting for Mr. Thompson to tell him it hadn't really happened. "That one," Mr. Thompson said, "you could show to a DMV examiner without bribery." Kristian demanded veracity, wanting to check the wheel angles against the notebook, but Madelyn ruled that the parking had been clean and that his records were, in this instance, irrelevant. Cole pulled out and did it again, slightly worse, then again, better, and the four of them stood in the cooling street arguing about whether consistency or brilliance counted more, which was the kind of argument they could keep alive for hours.

The next part Mr. Thompson refused to supervise, on the grounds that his heart was not young. Instead he rode along on the slow approach to the highway on-ramp, then directed Cole onto the interstate at one in the afternoon, when traffic was light enough to be forgiving. Cole merged at what felt like the speed of a paper airplane and then, once in the right lane, discovered that merging was not one skill but several: checking the mirror, the blind spot, the speedometer, the gap, all while the wheel wanted to drift. "You're doing the thing where you stare at one thing for a week," Mr. Thompson said. "Look where you want to go."

The real test came on the way home. A lane closure on the county highway had squeezed two lanes into one, and a line of cars sat motionless in the right lane while the left lane stood empty, its END warning sign visible maybe half a mile up. Cole signalled and began to move over early, and a truck behind them honked, long and personal. Kristian, in the back seat with Madelyn, leaned forward. "That guy seems bellicose," he said. "He wants the lane to himself."

"He wants us out of it," Madelyn said. "Everyone's taught to get over early, so they think anyone who uses the open lane is cheating." She'd read something, she said, from Minnesota's Department of Transportation: use both lanes right up to the merge point, then take turns, one car from each side. It's called the zipper merge, and it could cut the length of a backup by as much as 40 percent. Cole looked at the empty lane stretching ahead of them, at the sign, at the rearview mirror full of the honking truck.

"So the polite thing and the right thing are opposites," he said.

"Maybe the polite thing is just what everyone's used to," Madelyn said. "Maybe it's not the same as polite."

Cole held the wheel and did not signal. The empty lane ran beside them like an invitation written in a language he was only starting to read, and behind them the truck had inched closer, close enough that its grille filled the mirror. Mr. Thompson said, quietly, "Your call, driver." The END sign waited, half a mile up, and Cole eased off the brake.

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: Many US colleges fill waitlist spots in May, after admitted students have sent deposits and the college knows how many places are still open.
story:
The portal had been open for eleven minutes and Keira had read the sentence four times, as if the words might rearrange themselves into something kinder. "After careful review, we are unable to offer you a place in the incoming class at this time. You have been placed on our waitlist." She pushed back from the desk until her chair bumped the bed, then rolled forward again, because the screen was still there.

She called Noemie, who answered mid-bite of something.

"Say it in a normal voice," Noemie said. "Not your ghost voice."

"Waitlisted at Aldercrest."

There was a pause long enough for chewing. "Okay. So that's not a no."

"It's a maybe with no expiration date, which is worse. It's like a door that's neither locked nor unlocked."

"That's entropy, my friend. Doors decay. Everything decays." Noemie had adopted the word in physics class and now deployed it against every inconvenience, weather, slow Wi-Fi, her brother. Keira laughed despite herself, which she suspected was the point.

They looked it up together, Noemie reading aloud from her own screen while Keira followed along. The college's FAQ page was blandly unhelpful, all "we cannot predict," but a forum thread from a previous year laid it out plainly: many colleges fill waitlist spots in May, after admitted students have sent deposits and the college knows how many places are still open. Keira read it twice. "So they don't even look at the waitlist until after everyone's paid up somewhere."

"Paid up," Noemie said. "Past tense. Meaning you, potentially, paying a deposit somewhere else while you wait."

That was the trap, and they both saw it at the same moment, the way you see a step missing in a staircase. Keira had an acceptance from Marston, a good school, a school whose brochure had genuinely enthralled her mother, all brick and banners and a lake positioned precisely for photographs. The deposit was due the first of May. If she paid it and Aldercrest then called, she'd lose the money, which was real money, hers from two summers of scooping ice cream. If she didn't pay it and Aldercrest never called, she'd have nowhere to go at all.

"Coin flip?" Kayleb suggested at lunch the next day, producing an actual quarter.

"That's not a decision, that's a coin." But she took the quarter and turned it over in her fingers, because the weight of it, small and definite, was satisfying in a way the whole situation was not. "The thing is, I keep thinking if I just wait long enough, the answer will get clearer. But it won't. It gets clearer for the college. Not for me."

"Deep," said Kayleb. "Tangential, but deep."

"How is that tangential?"

"It's about colleges, not about you. You're the one holding the quarter."

Ms. Lavoie, who supervised the library during lunch, drifted past their table with a cart of returns and said, without stopping, "Aldercrest?" She had somehow absorbed the whole drama through the general atmosphere. "My niece waited off a list one year. Made a giant chart. Chart-making is not deciding, by the way. I say that with love." She shelved a book about marine mammals and kept going.

That night Keira sat at the computer with two tabs open, Marston's deposit page and the Aldercrest waitlist page, and made herself think it through instead of just feeling it through. The waitlist would not move until May, after deposits were in and the college could count its empty seats, so waiting longer bought her nothing but waiting. The uncertainty wasn't a fog that would lift; it was a structure, and she could see its shape now. If Aldercrest did call, it would be late, and losing a deposit was a cost she could survive. If she gambled everything on maybe and lost, there was no version of surviving that she liked. She thought about the ice cream summers, the smell of waffle cones baked into her skin, and thought, fine, that money exists to be spent on exactly this.

She typed the card number into Marston's page and pressed submit, and the confirmation banner appeared like a door that had, at last, been opened by someone decisive.

Then she opened her email and wrote to Aldercrest anyway, because the forum also said a short note reaffirming interest couldn't hurt. She kept it to three sentences. She read it aloud once, sent it, and closed the laptop with both hands, the way you close a piano.

From the hallway her mother called, "Did you decide something?"

"Marston," Keira called back. "For now. Probably. Ask me in May."

"May," her mother said, and Keira could hear the smile in it. "I'll buy a calendar."

activity: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
knowledge_domain: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
fact: US inflation peaked at 14.8 percent in March 1980 and fell below 3 percent by 1983, after the Federal Reserve's sharp interest rate increases.
story:
The lemonade stand stood at the end of Clara's driveway, a plywood counter her father had built when she was nine and never taken down. She had repainted it last summer, and now it held a pitcher, a cash box with exactly four dollars and a handful of nickels in it, and two textbooks. Dereck sat on an overturned milk crate across from her, fanning himself with the study sheet Mr. Hoffmann had handed out on Friday.

"Presentation Monday, first period," he said. "He literally said if we can't explain it to someone at a bus stop, we don't understand it."

"He said lemonade stand," Clara said. "He said that specifically." Mr. Hoffmann had been leaning against the doorframe when he said it, holding his coffee, looking at her in a way that suggested he already knew she was the one who would take him literally. She had texted Dereck within the hour.

A car slowed at the curb, a woman with a toddler in the passenger seat, and Clara poured a cup and made change, and when the car pulled away she wiped the counter and tried again. "So. Interest rates go up." She held her hands out like she was weighing two invisible things. "And then... people don't buy as much stuff." She heard how it sounded, flat, like a rule memorized in the five minutes before a test. Dereck's face said the same thing.

"That's not an explanation," he said. "That's a sentence with arrows missing."

"I know it. I know it in my head and it won't come out my mouth." She pulled the printout toward her, the graph Mr. Hoffmann had circled in red pen, and flattened the crease with the heel of her hand. The line climbed steeply through the late seventies, hit its peak, then dropped down the far side like a cliff. "Look. US inflation peaked at 14.8 percent in March 1980," she read. "And by 1983 it was below 3 percent."

"After the Fed raised rates," Dereck said, chewing the end of his pen. He had the numbers written on his forearm in green ink, which their teacher would probably notice. "So that's the thing we have to explain. That drop."

"But why is the drop there," Clara said, and then stopped, because an old man had walked up from the direction of the park, breathing hard, his shirt stuck to his back. Dereck poured without being asked, and Clara found the paper fan they kept under the counter for exactly this kind of customer, and the man sat on the crate Dereck vacated and drank half the cup in one motion.

"Hot enough to ionize the air," he said, waving the fan at his own face. "You could almost believe the sky's electric." He looked at the graph lying open between the pitcher and the napkins. "That's an ugly little mountain."

"That's inflation," Clara said. "Prices going up. In 1980 it got to almost fifteen percent, and then three years later it was under three, and I have to stand up Monday and say why."

The man snorted, not unkindly. "My brother bought a house that year. Nobody would lend to him after that but the rates, oh, the rates." He drained the cup and set a dollar on the counter, though the lemonade was fifty cents, and refused the change with a raised hand when Clara tried to give it back. "You kids take your time. Summer's long." He walked back toward the park at the same slow, stubborn pace.

Clara sat down in his vacated spot and stared at the graph. The line's collapse looked almost too clean, like something drawn afterward to make a point, and she mistrusted it for that. "My mom says raising rates is just making poor people pay more," she said. "She called it punishing the impecunious. She's been reading the news out loud at dinner." Dereck laughed at the word, and she laughed too, because her mother deployed vocabulary like that on purpose, a family elocution inherited from Clara's grandfather, words placed on the table like good silverware. "But Mr. Hoffmann says it's the main tool, and the graph says it worked, so."

"So both things can be true," Dereck said. "The drop is real, and your mom's mad about it."

"Maybe that's the whole answer." Clara traced the falling line with one finger. "Not why it works. I can say that part fine when I'm alone, borrowing costs, less spending, it's the practice that keeps failing. But Monday I could start here, with the numbers, 14.8 in March of 1980, under 3 by 1983, and then say the honest part, which is that it cost people something, and I'm not sure how you weigh that."

The afternoon thinned out. They sold three more cups, one to Abdul, who biked over from his shift at the pool and paid with quarters dripping chlorine-smelling water onto the counter, and who listened to Clara run the whole opening twice and told her the second run was better. By six the light had gone amber and the pitcher was down to its sugary last inch.

"Run it once more," Dereck said, stacking the cups. "The bus stop version."

Clara stood up behind the counter, wiped her palms on her shorts, and looked out at the empty street the way she would look at a classroom. "In March of 1980, inflation in the United States peaked at 14.8 percent. Three years later it was below 3 percent, after the Federal Reserve raised interest rates sharply. And I'm going to tell you what that did, and what it cost, and what I still can't decide about it."

"Say the last part again," Dereck said, "but slower."

activity: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
knowledge_domain: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
fact: Under joint and several liability, each of several people who share an obligation can be held responsible for the entire amount, not only their own share.
story:
The driving school on Delmore Avenue shared a parking lot with a bail bonds office, and Landon had started reading the bondsman's window while he waited for the evening class to unlock. Release, the flyer said, subject to terms and conditions. He liked the phrase without knowing why. It sounded like a promise with a trapdoor built into it.

Inside, the classroom smelled of burnt coffee and the rubber of floor mats. Mr. Kim, the instructor, was a dour man who read attendance as though sentencing people, and tonight he was going over the enrollment forms one last time before the road test on Friday. "You signed a waiver," he said, tapping the stack. "Check the box again if your parent also signed, because without a countersignature the school carries the liability and I carry the paperwork." Liability, Landon wrote in the margin of his notebook, next to a small doodle of a stop sign. The word kept surfacing all week, like a coin at the bottom of a pool he kept diving into.

The real deadline, though, was the apartment. Rehan had texted him at noon: the landlord wanted all three signatures, Landon's, Rehan's, Anaelle's, by Thursday at six, or the unit went to the next applicant. The three of them had found it in June, a third-floor walk-up with a kitchen window facing west, and Landon had spent the summer imagining his desk under that light. He wanted it the way you want something you have already furnished in your head.

Anaelle arrived at the driving school at the break, breathless, holding the lease against her chest like a shield. She and Rehan had read it at the coffee shop and had an argument about it, she said, a real one, and they needed Landon to be the tiebreaker because he was the one who read everything. He took the pages. The print was small and dry, and it seemed designed to desiccate any excitement a person might feel about a west-facing window. Clause 14 ran nearly half a page.

"Read the part I circled," Anaelle said.

He read it. Then he read it again, slower. Under the heading printed in bold capitals, the clause said that the tenants would be jointly and severally liable for the rent. He understood the first word immediately and the second one not at all, which bothered him in the specific way that an untranslated sentence bothers a person who thinks he is fluent. He looked up at Anaelle. "Do you know what 'severally' means here?"

"Rehan says it means separately. Like, severally. Severed. Each of us pays our share."

"That's what I would have guessed too," Landon said. But he had learned, from the waiver and from Mr. Kim's attendance sheet and from a summer of forms, that words in contracts kept their oldest meanings, not their obvious ones. He typed it into his phone. The screen lit his face in the dim classroom while the coffee machine hissed behind him.

The answer made him sit still for a moment. Jointly and severally liable meant that any one of them could be held responsible for the entire rent, not merely a third of it. If Rehan lost his job and Anaelle transferred schools, the landlord could come to Landon alone for the whole amount, every month, for the full term. "It's not three shares," he said out loud. "It's three whole obligations stacked on top of each other, and the landlord can pick whichever one of us is easiest to collect from." Anaelle sat down hard in the chair beside him. "So if you two bail, I'm the lease."

"Exactly. And I'm yours, if I'm the easy one."

Rehan came in ten minutes later, rain-damp, still holding the position from the coffee shop: they were best friends since seventh grade, no one was going to bail, the clause was for strangers. And Landon felt the pull of that, because it was true as far as it went. But he also thought about jurisprudence, a word he'd picked up from a documentary and liked precisely because it admitted that promises get tested in rooms where nobody knows anybody. Friendship was one kind of evidence. A signature was another, colder kind, made for the day the first kind runs out. He could not make the two into one. He could only look straight at the gap between them.

"Here's where I've landed," he said. "I still want the apartment. I'm not going to pretend the clause isn't there. So either we sign knowing any one of us could owe everything, and say that to each other out loud first, or we go to the landlord tomorrow and ask him to change it, and risk losing Thursday." Rehan began to argue that asking was the same as losing. Anaelle interrupted him, quietly. "Say the first part. That we each know we could be on the hook for all of it." Rehan looked at the floor mats, at the flyer in the window with its trapdoor promise, and then at them.

Mr. Kim reappeared in the doorway, jingling the keys, telling them the building closed at nine. Landon clicked his pen and signed his name once on the practice waiver, then again, testing how the second signature looked beside the first, as though each Landon might be answerable for the other. "We go tomorrow at noon," he said. "Together. Anaelle talks, I hold the lease."

activity: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
knowledge_domain: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
fact: Ignoring air resistance, a ball dropped from a table and a ball launched horizontally from the same height hit a level floor at the same time.
story:
The exam was at eight the next morning, and Vanessa had spread her notes across the kitchen table by seven in the evening, which left her thirteen hours, eight of which she intended to sleep. Mr. Schneider, whose apartment shared the building's thin ceiling with hers, had already knocked twice that week when her music ran past ten. She kept her voice low tonight, and when the doorbell rang at half past seven she signed at the peephole before opening it.

Naila came in carrying a paper bag of oranges and a physics textbook she clearly had not opened. Maram followed with a badminton racket, for reasons she did not explain. They had all three failed the last quiz, and the coach, who also taught their section, had made it plain that a second failure would cost them their places on the team, a disincentive that concentrated the mind better than any study schedule.

"The problem is the chapter," Naila said, dropping oranges onto the table among Vanessa's diagrams. "It keeps splitting everything into two. Horizontal this, vertical that. My brain wants one ball, one motion."

"You have to dichotomize it," Vanessa said. "That's the whole trick. The sideways part and the up-and-down part don't talk to each other."

"That sounds made up."

"It's in the notes. Look." She slid the page across. "For the horizontal part, the velocity never changes. For the vertical part, the ball speeds up as it falls, the same as if you just dropped it."

Maram picked up an orange and weighed it in her hand. "You could drop this from the table."

"With what next to it?"

"Another one, thrown sideways. Same height. Same time."

Naila sat back. "The thrown one has farther to travel. It'll take longer."

"It travels farther but it doesn't fall slower," Vanessa said, and then stopped, because saying it out loud she heard how much she was repeating rather than believing. The quiz had asked exactly this and she had answered wrong, and the red mark still sat in the margin of her notebook like a small dour face. "I think they land together. But I got it wrong once already, so."

"Then we test it," Maram said. She was already peeling an orange, which struck Vanessa as a waste of a perfectly spherical object, and so Vanessa went to the bowl by the window and took the last two, one for each hand.

They cleared the table. The kitchen floor was level linoleum, which mattered, though Vanessa could not have said why it mattered until she said it out loud: level floor, same height, that was the condition. She laid a ruler along the table edge to mark the drop point. Maram would hold the second orange at the same height and fling it sideways, straight out, parallel to the floor. The problem was timing. None of them trusted their eyes, and the flight would last less than a second.

"We don't watch," Naila said. "We listen."

The building was quiet except for the refrigerator. Vanessa stood by the table with her orange held over the mark, arm straight, and closed her eyes, which felt ridiculous and which she did anyway. Maram crouched at the far end of the table with hers. Naila knelt on the floor between them, eyes shut, one palm flat on the linoleum.

"On three," Vanessa said. "One, two, three."

Two sounds, close enough together that she could not order them, and then Naila, still kneeling, said, "Together. I felt it through the floor, once. One thump."

"You're guessing."

"I'm not. Drop them again."

They ran it four more times. On the second try Maram threw hers at an angle slightly downward, and Naila called that one unfair, a different experiment, so they agreed on rules: straight out, level with the tabletop, no push toward the floor. On the third and fourth runs the sounds came so close that Vanessa, listening with her whole body, heard what was either one impact or two pressed against each other. On the fifth, Maram threw hers hard enough that it crossed the kitchen and bounced off the cabinet, and from above came two knocks of Mr. Schneider's broom handle, unhurried and final.

They froze. Naila put a hand over her mouth. Maram whispered, "That's the ceiling."

"I know what it is."

The last orange rolled to rest against the cabinet. Vanessa picked it up and set it on the table, level with the drop mark, and stood looking at it for a moment. The thrown orange had crossed half the kitchen before landing, and it had landed when the dropped one did, every time she had actually listened. The sideways speed, then, whatever it was, did not hold the ball up or let it down. The two motions ran alongside each other, and the falling one kept its own time.

She pulled the quiz from her notebook and looked at the question she had missed. A ball rolls off a table at two meters per second; a second ball is dropped from the same edge at the same instant; ignoring air resistance, which lands first. She had written that the dropped ball lands first, since the thrown ball has more ground to cover. She took out a pen and, next to her wrong answer, wrote: they land at the same time. She did not write why. She was not certain she could yet, in the chapter's language, though she believed it now in the way that mattered, which was the way of five thumps on linoleum.

Naila read over her shoulder. "So on the exam, if they ask which lands first?"

"They both land first. Neither lands first. Same time."

"That's a terrible bet to offer someone."

"Then don't bet," Maram said. She had the badminton racket again and was sighting along it at the cabinet. "Bet on how far the thrown one goes instead."

Vanessa checked the clock. Twelve hours to the exam, and her notes still covered the table, and the last orange sat by the drop mark like evidence. From above came one more knock, softer, the kind that might have meant goodnight or might have meant stop, and Naila whispered, "Floor," and pointed down at the linoleum where the two dents in the dust still showed, side by side.

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: In the UK, students apply to university through UCAS and can choose up to five courses, listed in no order of preference.
story:
Tristan had taken the same table by the window every Tuesday since October, close enough to the socket that his laptop cord reached, far enough from the counter that Mr. Villanueva's espresso machine couldn't drown out his thoughts. He was there again, refreshing a page that hadn't changed since December, when Joy came in shaking rain off her jacket and dropped a folder the size of a phone book on his table.

"You got a minute?" she said. "Or ten. It's worse than you'd think."

She sat down without waiting for an answer and opened the folder. Inside were printouts, twelve of them, course descriptions from British universities, each one flagged with green and yellow sticky notes. She had already been accepted to a state school an hour from her house, she explained, a safety her mother loved and she tolerated, but she wanted the UK option kept open, and the deadline was in nine days.

"The problem is the form," she said. "It only lets you list five courses. Five. I've got twelve."

"Then cut seven," Tristan said.

"You cut seven." She spun the folder toward him. "Look at them. They're all the same thing, basically. History at Edinburgh, history at St Andrews, history and politics at Durham. If I cut any of them I'll spend the rest of my life wondering."

He read down the list while she went to the counter and ordered something with steamed milk. Mr. Villanueva wrote her name on a cup, got it wrong, and corrected it without comment. When she came back, Tristan tapped the folder.

"I did this in October," he said. "It's not as brutal as it looks. In the UK you apply through something called UCAS, and you can choose up to five courses, listed in no order of preference. All five go out the same way. The universities don't see which one you wanted most. Nobody sees. There's no ranking on the form at all."

Joy frowned at him. "So Edinburgh doesn't know it's my first choice?"

"It isn't anybody's first choice. That's the thing. There's no such field. You put down five and they're just five."

She sat with that for a moment, turning her cup so the lid's seam faced the window. "That's either the fairest system in the world or completely deranged," she said. "I've spent three days ranking these in a spreadsheet with weighted columns, and the form doesn't even care."

"It cares," Tristan said. "Just not about that part."

Kennedy arrived then, late and apologizing, carrying a paper bag of pastries she'd been sent to fetch for the debate team, which had colonized the long table by the door. She pulled up a chair, listened for ninety seconds, and began eating Joy's sticky notes in a manner of speaking, peeling off the least-defended printouts one at a time and asking Joy to defend each. Glasgow fell in under a minute. Trinity College Dublin was never eligible to begin with, being in Ireland, which Joy said she had known and Kennedy said she plainly had not.

Tristan watched rather than helped. His own list had taken one evening, five courses chosen with a confidence he now found almost embarrassing. What he hadn't reckoned on was the waiting, which turned out to be endemic to the whole business, everyone he knew either waiting or pretending not to wait. His parents asked about it every dinner. His coach asked about it every practice. He had started leaving his phone in his locker during workouts just to stop himself checking email between sets.

"You could rank them privately," Kennedy said. "Just for you. Write your order on a napkin, burn it, whatever. The system doesn't want to know but you still get to."

"Except then I'm subsuming five different futures into one ranked list," Joy said, "and the one I put first becomes the one I want just because I put it first. That's circular. That's like an oxymoron with extra steps."

"That's not what an oxymoron is," Kennedy said.

"It's close enough."

Tristan turned his laptop around so they could see the screen. The portal was still open, still blank where an answer would go. He had refreshed it that morning at 6:40, at lunch, and again when he sat down. Joy looked at it, then at him, and for a moment the whole college project felt less like a set of separate problems and more like one weather system they were all standing under.

"Any day now?" she asked.

"They say by May. Some people hear in March."

Joy closed her folder, having cut nothing, and asked Mr. Villanueva for a bigger table, one with room to spread twelve printouts across it. He cleared the corner booth and brought her a fresh coffee she hadn't ordered. Kennedy stole the first pastry out of the debate team's bag and slid half of it across to Tristan.

"Five," Joy said from the booth, pen in hand. "No order. I'm doing it right here, right now, and none of you get to vote."

Tristan closed his laptop, took a bite of the pastry, and watched her cross out Glasgow a second time, this time for keeps.

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: The secret printed ballot is called the Australian ballot because Australian colonies, Tasmania and Victoria, introduced it in 1856.
story:
Luca turned eighteen on the fourth of the month, and the county had mailed his ballot to the house eleven days before the election, so there was no excuse left. He set the envelope on the desk beside the keyboard, opened his laptop, and did not touch either one for a while. His father had already voted, had driven to the early polling place on Saturday and come back in twenty minutes, and had said nothing about it at dinner, which Luca understood to be the point.

He opened the envelope with a butter knife. Inside were two cards and a sleeve of stiff paper, and he laid them out under the desk lamp the way Ms. Nair had told the class to lay out an exam, everything parallel, nothing hidden. She had said that in September, before any of them could vote, and half the class had rolled their eyes. Luca had not, mostly because Kabir had leaned over and whispered that the midterm was an encumbrance on his freedom, and Kabir's acerbic delivery had made even Ms. Nair laugh.

The chat window was already open. You get it yet, Kabir had typed, an hour ago.

Luca typed back: got it. marking it now.

Good, Kabir wrote. Did you look at the judge races like I sent you.

He had looked. Kabir had sent three links about one of the judicial candidates, articles about a sentencing decision from four years ago, and had followed the links with a paragraph calling the man a menace and then, in the next message, calling him worse. Luca had read all three articles. Two of them were fair, and one was from a site whose comment section seemed to exist mainly to vilify anyone the editors disliked, and Luca had closed that tab and sat with the other two for a long time without deciding anything.

Kabir sent another message before Luca could reply. My dad says you can photograph your ballot and send it to prove you voted the right way. It's a thing people do.

There was a knock at the door, the light double knock that meant Cassandre, who had walked over from two streets down because she never rang the bell. Luca let her in and she took the chair by the window while he stayed at the desk, and she said her own ballot was still in her backpack, unmarked, and that she had come over because at her house the ballot was a public event. My mom wants to watch, she said. She wants to check. I said I'd rather do it somewhere else.

Luca looked at the two cards under the lamp. Nobody's supposed to see it, right, he said. Like legally.

It's called the Australian ballot, Cassandre said. We did it in Ms. Nair's class. The secret printed ballot. Australia came up with it first, the colonies, Tasmania and Victoria, in 1856.

Huh, Luca said. He turned that over. So the whole secrecy thing isn't even old. There was a time when everybody watched everybody mark it.

Apparently, Cassandre said. She pulled her backpack onto her knees but did not take out her ballot. Kabir keeps texting you.

He does, Luca said. He wants me to send a photo of it when I'm done. Proof I voted right. He typed as he spoke, telling Kabir the ballot was secret for a reason, and that people had set that up on purpose, and that he wasn't sending anything.

Kabir's reply came fast. it's not about you it's about the judges race. that guy is genuinely dangerous. if you're not with this you're basically for him.

Luca read it twice. He thought about the third article, the one with the comment section, and about how Kabir had been the person in their grade who stood up in assemblies, and how standing up and this were not the same thing, and how he could not find the exact line between them. He typed: I read the articles. I'm not telling you how I marked anything. That's the deal now. Sorry.

Kabir did not reply. The chat showed him typing, then not typing, then typing again, and then nothing at all.

Cassandre had her ballot out of the backpack, flat on her knees, a pen uncapped. She looked at the window rather than at Luca. Can I do it here, she said. Not like you watching. Just like somebody in the room.

Yeah, Luca said. He picked up his own pen. He marked the first card, folded it into the sleeve, and then sat with the second card, the judges, the race Kabir cared about, for what Cassandre would later describe as a full two minutes, pen in the air, the lamp buzzing faintly. Then he marked it, folded it, sealed the envelope, and signed the outside, and Cassandre did the same with hers, and neither of them looked at the other's paper.

She held her sealed envelope up to the light, once, and laughed at herself, and put it in her backpack. They took Luca's ballot out to the mailbox together at the corner of the street. The flag on the box was up already, somebody else's mail waiting. Luca put his envelope in, pushed the flag down, and stood there with his hand still resting on the cold metal. So, Cassandre said. Want to go back and see if Kabir wrote anything?

activity: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
knowledge_domain: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
fact: TinEye, a reverse image search engine launched in 2008, can sort results with the oldest first, helping find when an image first appeared online.
story:
Loic had the video queued on the big television before anyone else arrived, which was how he liked it: the living room rearranged, the lamp angled away from the screen, two bowls of chips because one was never enough. The clip showed a flooded street with a car half submerged, a caption in urgent capitals about a dam failing two states away, and beneath it a counter ticking upward, thirty thousand shares in four hours. He had already sent it to his group chat with a single word, "jesus," before Kirsten knocked.

"Take it down," she said. She didn't sit. She stood between him and the screen with her phone held out, and on it was the same flooded street, the same half-drowned car, dated six years earlier.

"That's impossible, it's from today." But even as he said it he was scrolling back through his own messages, and the certainty he'd felt an hour ago, warm and self-important, began to feel like something borrowed from strangers. Nika arrived in the middle of this, dropped onto the far end of the couch, and asked what they were fighting about, in the tone of someone who hoped it was juicy.

"Loic spread a fake," Kirsten said.

"I didn't fake anything. I shared what I saw." He hated how defensive it came out, and he hated more that the distinction he was defending, between making a lie and passing one along, seemed thinner every second he looked at it. Nika, insouciant as ever about other people's crises, was already eating the chips. Then she leaned forward.

"My brother does this thing," she said. "Reverse image search. You put the picture in and it finds where it's been. TinEye, it's called. It came out in 2008. You can sort the results with the oldest first." She said it the way she reported most things, flatly, as though everyone's brother were an autodidact who hoarded verification tricks the way other people hoarded memes.

Loic pulled his laptop off the side table and opened the site. Uploading the still frame took longer than the moment deserved; Kirsten stood behind the couch with her arms folded, and he could feel her watching his hands. The results loaded. He clicked the oldest-first sort, and there it was, the same photograph, posted years before the flood it supposedly portended, on a page about a different disaster in a different decade. Not recycled footage of a real event, but a photograph that had outlived its own truth, migrating from tragedy to tragedy, gathering urgency with each move.

"So delete it," Kirsten said, softer now, because the fight had gone out of the room and left something else behind.

He deleted the message from the chat. Then, before he could talk himself out of it, he posted a correction, which felt strangely like confessing to a crime he hadn't intended to commit, and a few people liked it, and one person replied with a shrug emoji, and Mr. Hamdan, his old neighbor, who was always in the group chat and never in the conversation, typed a single thumbs up. Nika pointed at the screen and laughed at the shrug emoji as if it were the funniest thing she'd seen all week. Loic turned back to the laptop and ran the other image through TinEye too, the one from last month he'd shared without thinking, watching the results sort themselves oldest first, and waiting to find out how much of what he'd passed along had ever been true at all.

activity: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
knowledge_domain: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
fact: A 1990 follow-up of Mischel's preschoolers found that those who had waited longer for the second treat tended to have higher SAT scores as teenagers.
story:
Kyle arrived at Ms. Perera's classroom four minutes early, which was unusual, and sat with his chair pushed back from the table as though he might still leave. On the desk in front of him lay two envelopes, one thin and one thick, and he kept his hand on the thick one as if it might slide away on its own.

"You're the first one here," Ms. Perera said, arranging mugs. She ran these Thursday mentorship meetings for juniors, three or four students at a time, mostly so they would have somewhere to say things out loud that the cafeteria drowned out. "Misha and Ocean are coming?"

"Probably." Kyle turned the thick envelope over. It had arrived Tuesday, and he had opened it alone in his room, and he had not told anyone at school yet, not even Ocean, who had been the first to know about everything since seventh grade, including the time he broke his wrist on the trampoline and told everyone it happened saving a dog.

He had not told anyone because telling made it real, and if it was real he had to decide.

Misha came in with rain on her jacket and Ocean a minute behind, arguing already about a teacher who had moved a test without warning. They settled around the table, and Ms. Perera poured tea that tasted like somebody's garden, and for a while the talk was ordinary, the ordinary biome of junior year, as Misha called it once: homework, the cross-country coach's moods, whether the vending machine on the second floor took bills anymore.

"Kyle has something," Misha said, because she noticed things like that. "He's doing the envelope thing."

Kyle set both envelopes in the middle of the table. The thin one was from the state university, close enough to live at home, with a scholarship that covered almost everything. The thick one was from a summer program at a university two states away, the kind with laboratories and professors and a price that would eat the money his mother had been saving since he was small, the money she called the just-in-case fund.

"Six weeks," he said. "It's six weeks and it costs what she saved. And I keep thinking about this thing I heard at the open house in March."

Ocean leaned forward. "What thing?"

"There was this dad there," Kyle said, "waiting for the tour with his daughter, and he starts talking to me while we're in line for coffee. He said a 1990 follow-up of Mischel's preschoolers found that the kids who had waited longer for the second treat tended to have higher SAT scores as teenagers."

"Preschoolers," Misha said. "Mischel's preschoolers? What did they wait for?"

"Marshmallows. Or whatever the treat was. They could eat one now or wait and get two later. That's all he said. Then his daughter dragged him off to the engineering building." Kyle turned his mug a quarter turn, then another quarter. "The dad was being kind of effusive about it, like it explained everything, like the whole future comes down to one afternoon when you're four."

Nobody spoke for a moment. Rain moved against the windows, and down the hall a janitor's cart squeaked and stopped.

"So that's the question," Kyle said. "That's what I can't get out of my head. If waiting for a second treat at four says something about you at seventeen, then the money is the treat, right? If I wait, if I don't spend it now, it's there later, for actual college, for the real thing. The thin envelope is the waited-for thing. But the program is also the smart choice, the ambitious choice, the thing everyone says you do if you get the chance. Both of them are waiting for something. I can't figure out which one is the marshmallow."

Ms. Perera, who had been listening with her hands folded, said only, "What did the study actually compare? Say it back exactly."

"The kids who waited longer," Kyle said slowly, "tended to have higher SAT scores. Tended to. It's not one kid, it's all of them averaged." He stopped. He heard what he had said. "So it's not about any single afternoon."

"It's not about yours either," Misha said quietly.

He recalibrated, there at the table, and it felt like the room shifting a few degrees. Maybe the marshmallow study wasn't an instruction, a formula where you identified the treat and held out and got rewarded. Maybe it was a description of a lot of small moments all leaning the same way, and no single choice carried the whole weight of who he'd be at twenty-five. That was both a relief and a heavier thing, because it meant the program wouldn't save him and skipping it wouldn't ruin him, and there was no study that could tell him what his mother's face would do when he showed her the cost.

"Can I be honest?" he said. "I still don't know. I keep flip-flopping, and part of me wants one of you to just tell me."

"I'll tell you what I know," Ocean said. "Your mom cried when you made regionals. Good cried. She'd cry either way."

"That's not deciding for me."

"No," Ocean said. "It's not."

Ms. Perera looked at the clock. "We have ten minutes. Why don't you tell us what the program actually is, day to day. Not what it means. What you'd do at nine in the morning."

Kyle pulled the thick envelope back toward himself and opened it again, all the way this time, and spread the pages across the table where Misha and Ocean could read them, his finger moving down the schedule to the first line of the first day.

activity: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
knowledge_domain: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
fact: Ignoring air resistance, the horizontal distance a projectile travels equals its constant horizontal velocity multiplied by its time in the air.
story:
The physics worksheet had followed Hayden into the science museum, folded into his back pocket like a warrant. Ms. Sok had assigned it that morning, twelve projectile problems, and had told the class that if they finished early at the museum they could use the exhibits however they liked. He had not finished early. He had finished nothing.

The ballistics exhibit sat at the center of the second floor, a long clear chamber with an air cannon at one end and a grid of glowing targets along the far wall. You set the launch angle and the speed, the machine fired a foam ball, and the wall recorded where it struck. Meriem was already there, tapping the angle controls with the patience of someone defusing a bomb, and Abigayle stood beside her with her phone out, filming misses.

"You're supposed to be doing the worksheet," Hayden said.

"I am doing the worksheet. Experientially." Meriem set the angle to thirty degrees and the speed to its lowest notch. The ball sailed, thudded into the wall a foot below the nearest target, and Abigayle lowered her phone in something close to grief.

Hayden pulled the worksheet out. Problem four: a ball launched at a known speed and angle, asking for the horizontal distance it travels before landing. He had circled it twice on the bus. He understood that a launched object had a velocity, and he understood gravity pulled it down, but somewhere between those two facts his reasoning collapsed, and every time he tried to combine them he got a tangle that belonged to neither the sky nor the ground.

Meriem leaned over his shoulder. "You're doing what I did for an hour. You're treating the diagonal as one thing."

"It is one thing. It's the ball."

"Watch," she said, and fired again. The ball rose, hung for a heartbeat near the top of its arc, and dropped. "It's one ball doing two jobs at once. Up and down, which gravity keeps messing with, and across, which nothing touches. The across part just... keeps going. Same speed the whole flight."

Hayden stared at the chamber. The flight time, that was something he could get; the up and down part was the part with the clean equations, the ones he actually understood. On problem four he had already found the time in the air, forty seconds of work abandoned at the last line because he hadn't known what to do with it. Now he looked at the ball's horizontal speed, which on his paper was a constant number, and at the time, another constant number, and something turned over in his chest, quiet and visceral, like a key finding its lock. Ignore everything except across, multiply across by time, and you got exactly where it landed. He did it in the margin. The answer came out to a number that meant something, an actual spot on actual ground.

"I need to check it," he said.

They took over the controls. Meriem worked the problem backward with him, reading numbers off his page, and they set the cannon's speed and angle to match. The chamber had marks along its floor, and Hayden knelt at the edge counting them while Abigayle, pressed against the glass, called the arc like a race announcer. The ball launched, rose, hung, fell, and bounced twice before rolling to a stop.

"Where?" Meriem demanded.

Hayden measured with his shoe, heel to toe, from the firing line to the ball. Then he looked at his margin. "It landed where the math said. Not close. On it."

"That's the twist, by the way," Abigayle said. "I filmed your face. You looked like the ball personally apologized to you."

But the twist that mattered came later, and it was not a comfort. At the gift shop, waiting for Ms. Sok to gather the stragglers, Hayden found a small plaque by the window describing the exhibit, and it credited a twelfth-century writer who had reasoned about thrown stones and falling water, separating motion into parts centuries before anyone wrote it in symbols. Meriem read it over his shoulder. "So we just did what some monk figured out watching rocks." Hayden nodded slowly, and the thought settled in him without resolving: the math worked, the ball obeyed it, and yet he could not have said why the across part stays untouched, only that it does, and that someone had trusted it long before he did. He folded the worksheet back into his pocket, creased side out, all twelve problems waiting, and as the group moved toward the buses he said, "Give me the worksheet on the ride home. I want to try problem five without the cannon."

activity: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
knowledge_domain: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
fact: Georges Lefebvre's 1939 book, translated as The Coming of the French Revolution, described 1789 as four revolutions: aristocratic, bourgeois, urban popular and peasant.
story:
The Wi-Fi at his grandfather's house reached only as far as the kitchen table, so Victor carried his notebook out to the porch where the signal died entirely and he would have to think instead of search. The assignment had been hanging over him since spring break began: two thousand words on how views of the French Revolution had changed since 1800, and he had written, so far, one sentence. Ms. Silva-Jayasuriya had read that sentence aloud to the whole seminar, not cruelly, but in a way that made everyone hear how it said nothing. "The French Revolution has been interpreted in many ways," she had repeated, and then set the page down and looked at him until he understood that she was not going to rescue him.

His grandfather was in the garden pulling bindweed from the beans, an ascetic routine he kept even in the August heat, refusing gloves, refusing the stool Victor's mother had bought him. From the porch Victor could hear the roots tearing loose one at a time. Last summer he had spent the same two weeks here doing nothing, floating in the pond with Gianluca and Lyna until the light went, and he had chosen this summer's exile himself, telling his mother he needed quiet to work. He had not anticipated how quiet could press back.

He had brought four books, three of them from the school library, and by noon he had read enough to know that historians had argued about the Revolution the way his grandparents' neighbors argued about the property line, with maps and shouting and long silences. The Marxists said one thing. The revisionists, whoever they were exactly, said another. His notes had turned into two columns of claims that contradicted each other, and he could not make them sit in the same paragraph. He texted Gianluca a photo of the notebook spread open and got back a single thumbs up, which was its own kind of message.

It was his grandfather who disturbed him, coming up the porch steps with soil under his nails and a glass of lemonade Victor hadn't asked for. His grandfather did not ask about the essay. He asked whether Victor remembered the summer they had repainted the shed, and Victor said he did, though what he remembered was his grandfather letting him choose the color, an absurd blue, and defending it to Victor's mother. "You picked a direction and I let you live with it," his grandfather said, and went inside, and Victor sat with that for a while without deciding what it meant.

In the fourth book, the one with the cracked spine that smelled of his grandfather's study, he found what he had been circling. Georges Lefebvre, 1939, translated as The Coming of the French Revolution. Victor read the passage twice, then a third time, and then, because saying things out loud helped him keep them, he said it to the empty porch. "Lefebvre said 1789 was four revolutions. Aristocratic, bourgeois, urban popular, peasant." Four at once, overlapping, each with its own actors and its own stakes, happening inside the single word revolution that Victor had been treating like one thing.

He opened his notebook and drew four quick lines down the margin, and suddenly the two quarreling columns of his notes had somewhere to go. The historians were not simply disagreeing about one event; they were looking at different revolutions inside it, or weighting them differently, or blaming different ones. He did not yet know if that was exactly right. He tried drafting the paragraph, and in the middle of it he caught himself doing the thing Ms. Silva-Jayasuriya had flagged before, smoothing over a gap with a confident phrase. He crossed it out and wrote instead that the question of which revolution mattered most was the question the historians had been fighting over all along. That felt more honest and also less finished, and he let it stand.

That evening Lyna called from the city, her voice tinny against the sound of a party he had chosen not to attend. She asked what the pond was like and he told her the water level was low, and then, without planning to, he told her about the four revolutions, hearing the words come out uncertain at the edges, the way they do when you're testing whether you believe them. She said it sounded like the whole thing had been seismic in four directions at once, and he liked that, and wrote it in the margin, and then worried it was too good, borrowed rather than earned. He put a question mark beside it.

Before bed he read the new paragraph to his grandfather, who was shellings beans on the kitchen table and listening with the courtesy of a man who had lived through enough history to distrust all summaries of it. When Victor finished, admitting that he still didn't know whether Lefebvre's way of splitting things up solved his problem or just renamed it, his grandfather set down a bean and considered.

"Four revolutions," his grandfather said. "And you're only writing about one country?"

Victor looked at the notebook, at the four lines in the margin and the question mark he hadn't erased, and pulled the pencil back out from behind his ear.

activity: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
knowledge_domain: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
fact: A useful way to predict temperature effects is to treat heat as a product of an exothermic reaction and as a reactant of an endothermic one.
story:
The chemistry lab was in the subterranean wing of the school, windowless, and by October Violet had learned to dread the hour she spent in it, not because she disliked the subject but because equilibrium had quietly defeated her. She could shift a reaction with concentration, with pressure, could recite the answers the way you recite lines for a play you've never understood. Temperature was different. Temperature moved something she couldn't see, and every time Mr. Vu wrote a heated arrow on the board, she copied it down and felt nothing connect.

"You look like someone waiting for a bus that already came," Jacey said, sliding onto the stool beside her. Thursday, before the quiz, the room smelling faintly of someone's burnt hair from third period.

"I get everything except temperature. Hot water, cold water, which way it goes. I just guess and get it backwards half the time."

"That's the half that matters," Jacey said, and shrugged, and started labeling her axis, and Violet understood that this was Jacey's way of withdrawing, of not being asked to fix it. There had been a summer, two summers ago, when Jacey would have explained it three ways without being asked. Now there was a politeness between them, a border neither of them had named.

The quiz came back Monday with a 71 at the top, and Mr. Vu paused at her desk just long enough for the pause itself to say something. He didn't lecture. He set a worksheet down and moved on, and Violet sat with her 71 and a slow ennui that wasn't quite sadness, more like the flatness of a road with no turns. She had wanted this class. She had chosen it over art, which her mother still brought up at dinner in a voice that made the choosing sound like a betrayal, and Violet had stopped defending herself because defending herself to her mother was like arguing with weather. But she did sometimes wonder whether she had disenfranchised some earlier version of herself, the one who drew hands and doorways, whether that girl had lost a vote she was never allowed to cast.

That weekend her grandfather's house. Her mother dropped her there for the afternoon with a casserole dish, and her grandfather, who had taught chemistry for thirty years in a district where the labs had open flames, watched her spread the worksheet across his kitchen table next to the sugar bowl. "This one," she said, tapping the problem. "They heat it, and I'm supposed to say which way it shifts, and I don't know why I keep getting it wrong." He didn't explain. He had a rule about not explaining, which used to infuriate her and which she was beginning, this year, to find almost generous. He just drank his tea and said, "Write it out."

So she wrote the equation, and stared at it, and stared at it, with the radiator ticking under the window. And then, without deciding to, she picked up her pencil and added a word after the products. Heat. Just wrote it in, as if it belonged there, as if the reaction manufactured warmth the way it manufactured the compound on the right. And suddenly the problem made sense: adding heat was adding a product, and the system pushed back the way it always pushed back. She tried a second equation and wrote heat on the left instead, before the arrow, because this one soaked up warmth when it ran, and cooling it meant removing a reactant. It was a trick, she suspected. Some teacher's clever bookkeeping device. But the guesses stopped being guesses.

"Exothermic," her grandfather said, reading over her shoulder. "That's the kind where the heat comes out. Endothermic is the kind that takes it in." She nodded and kept writing, because if she stopped to talk about it she might lose the thread, and because she had learned, that year, that some things dissolve when you examine them too closely.

On Monday she found Abhijot in the hallway before first period, the one person in the class who asked questions that made Mr. Vu pause. "For temperature," she said, "you just write heat into the equation. Product if it's exothermic, reactant if it's endothermic. Then it's the same rules as everything else." Abhijot looked at her for a second, then at his notes, then did it, right there against the lockers, pencil moving.

At lunch Jacey asked how the retake went, and Violet said she thought she'd gotten the temperature questions right, all of them, and then hesitated, because "thought" was the honest word and she wanted to let it stand. Jacey waited, and for a moment the border between them thinned, and Violet almost told her about the kitchen table, the sugar bowl, the word she had written in. Instead she said, "Ask me tomorrow," and folded the retake slip into her pocket, creasing it flat.

activity: the idea that scientific consensus forms through repeated studies, peer review and replication rather than one result
knowledge_domain: the idea that scientific consensus forms through repeated studies, peer review and replication rather than one result
fact: A Danish study published in 2019 followed more than 650,000 children and found no link between the MMR vaccine and autism, even among children with autistic siblings.
story:
Seth had forty minutes before his mother picked him up, and the county library's reference computer still logged you off after thirty, so he typed fast. The assignment was a short paper for health class: pick a claim circulating online and trace where it came from. He'd picked the one his uncle had repeated at Thanksgiving, that the MMR vaccine caused autism. His uncle had said it like a secret everyone else was too polite to mention.

He found the source quickly, which surprised him. It traced back to a 1998 paper in a British medical journal, twelve children, and a doctor whose license was later taken away. Seth wrote the numbers on a yellow legal pad: twelve. Then, because the paper's retraction had spawned a hundred follow-up arguments, he kept digging, and the follow-ups were the part that interested him. There were studies from Poland, from Japan, from Canada. There was a meta-analysis combining several of them. It was like watching twelve pebbles get dropped into a pond and then watching the pond not move.

Alayna appeared over his shoulder with a granola bar and no plans to leave. "What are you doing?"

"Trying to figure out how many studies it takes to prove something." He scrolled. "This one's from Denmark."

She pulled a chair around backwards and sat on it the wrong way. "Prove how?"

He read the abstract slowly, once, and then again because the number kept sliding off his attention. "A Danish study published in 2019 followed more than 650,000 children and found no link between the MMR vaccine and autism." He tapped the screen. "Even among children with autistic siblings."

"Even them?"

"Even them. Which is the group you'd most expect to show it, if it were there."

Alayna unwrapped her granola bar with the deliberate calm of someone stalling. "So it's over. Twelve versus six hundred fifty thousand. Case closed."

But Seth was staring at a different tab, one he'd opened before she sat down, where a blogger had dismissed every large study as part of a cover-up and called one researcher a shill. The blogger wrote with a scathing confidence, every sentence a verdict, and Seth noticed his own pulse picking up as he read it, the way a certain kind of certainty can cauterize doubt before it even forms. He closed the tab. Not because the man was wrong about everything necessarily, but because the writing gave him nothing to check.

"Here's my problem," Seth said. "It's not twelve against six hundred fifty thousand. It's twelve against six hundred fifty thousand and I don't know how to count the second one. Is it one study? Is it ten? If they all say the same thing, does that make it stronger or does that mean they're copying each other?"

Mr. Silva-Jayasuriya, the reference librarian, stopped his cart beside their table on his way to shelving. He didn't offer wisdom, which Seth appreciated; he asked what database they'd used, then pointed at the screen. "See that line, 'peer reviewed'? It means other researchers read it before it was published and tried to find the mistakes." He tapped the masthead. "The rest of your answer is in that word, 'replication.' Other people ran it again." Then he moved on to the shelving, because he was a man who believed in finishing his cart.

Seth wrote the word down. Replication. On the pad it sat next to his columns, and he drew an arrow from it to the Polish study and the Japanese study and the Canadian one, then stopped, because he wasn't sure the arrow meant anything. Maybe each study was its own thing and the arrow was his invention. Maybe that was the point, that nobody had ever proven anything alone; they'd just kept asking and kept getting the same answer until the asking itself became the evidence. But he'd read enough of the blogger to know that a person who wanted to disbelieve could call that conspiracy instead of consensus, and Seth couldn't think of a clean way to tell the two apart from the outside. He could weigh the numbers. He couldn't weigh motives.

"I still have eight minutes," he said.

"Then stop philosophizing and start the paper." Alayna turned the legal pad toward herself, borrowed his pen, and wrote at the top of a fresh page, in handwriting much neater than his: "How do we know what we know?" She slid it back across the table. "Mr. Silva-Jayasuriya says the printer's free today."

Seth saved his sources, and under Alayna's question he wrote his first sentence: "In 1998, twelve children were enough to start a panic, and it took more than 650,000 to begin ending one." The countdown clock on the computer turned red. He hit print.

activity: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
knowledge_domain: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
fact: The derivative of a constant is zero, so adding 7 to a function shifts its graph up but leaves its derivative unchanged.
story:
Kyle was the last one through the door of Room 214, and Ms. Lin had already written a function on the board in her small, exact handwriting. The math club met on Thursdays after last bell, when the hallway smelled of floor wax and the radiators ticked like something counting. There were seven of them, and the desks had been pushed into a crooked horseshoe. Ms. Lin said only, "Differentiation. Find the slope at any point on a curve. Then tell me where the curve peaks." She put a worksheet face-down on each desk and sat by the window with her coffee, which was her way of saying the room belonged to them.

Kyle turned his paper over. His function was a polynomial, something with an x-squared term and a constant at the end. Below it, a blank box for the derivative, and then a question: where does the function reach its maximum? He had read the chapter twice the night before, lying on his bed with the textbook propped against his knees, and it had exhilarated him in a way he didn't quite want to admit at school, the idea that a curve could be interrogated, that you could take its slope like a pulse.

He worked the derivative the way the book said, term by term. Across the horseshoe, Adriano was hunched over his own sheet, pen tapping. Corinne sat with her ankles crossed under her chair, already finished, watching the two of them with an expression Kyle thought of as sardonic but probably was just patient.

"Mine's wrong," Adriano announced. "Or hers is."

Ms. Lin didn't look up from her coffee. "Why?"

Adriano stood, carried his worksheet to the board, and copied his derivative next to Corinne's, which she had written there without asking. Kyle left his seat and stood between them. The two derivatives on the board were identical, symbol for symbol, every coefficient the same.

"That's impossible," Adriano said. "Different functions can't have the same derivative. One of us dropped something."

Kyle pulled both original worksheets toward him and laid them side by side on the ledge of the chalkboard. The functions weren't identical. His own had a 7 at the end, a lone constant tacked on after the x-squared term; Corinne's didn't. He stared at the two sheets until the numbers stopped being numbers and started being a shape in his head, one graph floating above the other like a floor and its ceiling.

"Wait," Kyle said. "The 7 doesn't do anything to the derivative." He said it slowly, testing the sentence as he went. "Adding 7 shifts the whole graph up. But the derivative doesn't change.
