The derivative of a constant is zero." He copied the constant's derivative beside it on the board, a small flat 0, and stepped back.

Corinne tilted her head. "So we both did it right."

"So one of us did a pointless step," Adriano said, but he was grinning now, and Kyle understood, in a way he couldn't yet put into words, that the pointless step wasn't pointless, that it told you something about what a derivative could see and what it was blind to.

They went back to the maximum. Kyle set the derivative equal to zero and solved, and the x-value fell out clean. He plugged it back into his original function, with its 7, and got his height. Corinne plugged the same x-value into hers, without the 7, and got hers. Same peak, vertically. Two different ceilings, one floor.

Adriano looked between the two answers and said, "It's like speciation. Same slope-ancestors, different functions drifting apart." Kyle laughed, short and surprised, because it was a terrible analogy and also exactly right, and he was still deciding which it was more of.

When Ms. Lin finally collected the worksheets, she paused over Kyle's page, where he had written in the margin, "does the derivative forget the 7, or does it never see it?" She underlined nothing, corrected nothing, only folded the stack in half. Outside the window the parking lot was emptying, headlights sweeping the fence. Kyle zipped his backpack and asked Corinne, "Same time Thursday?" and she was already halfway to the door when she said, "Bring a harder one."

activity: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
knowledge_domain: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
fact: In The Great Gatsby, published in 1925, the narrator Nick Carraway says, 'I am one of the few honest people that I have ever known.'
story:
The porch at his grandmother's house still smelled of the pipe tobacco his grandfather had given up three years ago, as if the wood had sutured the smell into its grain and refused to let the habit die entirely. Brayden sat on the top step with The Great Gatsby open on his knees, the same cracked paperback his mother had read in college, and tried to figure out why he distrusted the man telling him the story.

"Nick Carraway," he said to Sydney, who was stretched across the wicker chair with her own copy balanced on her stomach. "He keeps saying he reserves judgment. He says it twice in the first chapter, like he's rehearsing it."

Sydney tilted her sunglasses down. "So?"

"So people who actually reserve judgment don't announce it." He flipped pages, hunting for the sentence he'd underlined without knowing why. "Here. He says, 'I am one of the few honest people that I have ever known.' The book came out in 1925, and this guy is telling us, point blank, that he's honest."

Dimitri arrived then, coasting his bike down the gravel drive with one foot dragging, and dropped onto the step below Brayden. "Grandmother still doing the book club?" he asked. He'd only come for the lemonade, but the books had a way of pulling him in.

"It's us," Sydney said. "We're the book club. Three members. Attendance mandatory."

Brayden read the quote aloud again, and something about hearing it in the open air changed it. At school, Ms. Li had asked them to consider how point of view shapes what a reader believes, and he'd written half a paragraph about it, the kind of inchoate answer that filled space without saying anything. Here, with the bees working the flower boxes and his grandmother's radio drifting through the screen door, the question felt sharper. If the narrator declares his own honesty, who is he trying to convince?

He grabbed a napkin from the lemonade tray and started listing moments where Nick bent things. "He says he's disgusted with everyone at the end, but he also spends the whole summer at their parties. He claims he hardly knows Jordan Baker, then dates her. He tells us Tom is a brute and then keeps having lunch with him." Each item went on the napkin in his cramped handwriting. "Either he's lying to us or he's lying to himself, and I honestly can't tell which is worse."

"Maybe both," Sydney said, sitting up. "Maybe that's the trick. You can't check his story against anything because he's the only one telling it." She paused. "Although if you accuse him, you're using his own evidence. He gave you the rope."

Dimitri squinted at the napkin. "So what's the answer for Ms. Li's essay? Trust him or not?"

Brayden looked at the list, then at the book, then at the yard where the light was going amber. He had wanted a verdict, a clean line he could write at the top of a page, and the book kept refusing to hand him one. Maybe that was the point, or maybe it was a failure of his own reading; he couldn't decide, and he noticed that the uncertainty itself felt almost enjoyable, like standing at a door he hadn't known was there. "Both, I think," he said slowly. "I trust what he sees and I don't trust what he says about himself. Those are different things."

"That's not an answer," Dimitri said.

"It's two answers," Brayden said, "and they don't like each other."

Sydney laughed, and his grandmother came out with a fresh pitcher, setting it down beside the napkin full of evidence. She looked at the scribbled list, then at the three of them, and said nothing, only filled their glasses to the brim.

Brayden folded the napkin into his copy of the book, pressing it flat between the pages where Nick made his claim, and closed the cover on it.

activity: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
knowledge_domain: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
fact: In England, the Tenant Fees Act 2019 caps most tenancy deposits at five weeks' rent when the annual rent is under £50,000.
story:
The open house was on Marlowe Street, a narrow brick terrace with a hand-lettered sign taped to the door, and Blake had walked there from school with Pablo and Maelys because Maelys had an appointment to view the bedsit upstairs and refused to go alone. The lettings agent stood in the hall holding a clipboard, and the landlord, a man with a ring of keys on his belt, leaned against the banister explaining the terms to a young woman who had arrived before them. Blake hung back by the door frame, where the smell of fresh paint was strongest, and listened.

"Deposit is two months' rent, upfront, plus first month," the landlord said. "Standard."

The young woman, who had a folder of printed pages under her arm, frowned at her phone. "Two months is eight weeks, give or take. That's not standard, is it?"

"Two months, and we sign Friday," the landlord said, in the tone of a man closing a conversation.

Maelys stepped forward. She was seventeen and had been researching flats since February with the intensity other people reserved for exams. "There's a thing called the Tenant Fees Act," she said. "In England, if the annual rent is under fifty thousand pounds, the deposit's capped at five weeks' rent. Most tenancies, anyway."

The landlord looked at her, then at the agent, who studied his clipboard as though it had suddenly become interesting. "Five weeks," the agent admitted, not looking up.

Blake had come along as moral support, and had expected to spend the visit waiting by the wall while Maelys argued numbers. Instead he found himself doing arithmetic on the back of the flyer, because the flyer listed the rent as nine hundred a month and he wanted to see what five weeks actually meant in pounds. Maelys leaned over his shoulder. "Annual rent's ten thousand eight hundred," she said. "Under the fifty. So the cap applies."

"Five weeks of two-oh-seven a week is about one thousand and thirty-five," Blake said. "Not the sixteen hundred he asked her for."

The young woman exhaled, and the sound of it made Blake aware that she had probably been holding her breath since Friday, maybe since she'd wired herself into believing she had no choice. She wrote the number down. "I checked the rules last night," she said, mostly to Maelys. "I just needed someone to say it out loud in front of him."

The landlord began to pontificate about wear and tear, about the last tenant who had burned a hob ring, about how deposits protected decent landlords from the recklessness of the young. Pablo, who had been examining the kitchen taps with theatrical suspicion, muttered, "He could just say he wanted the extra money," and Blake had to turn his cough into a clearance of the throat.

Ms. Rossi, who lived two doors down and had come over out of neighbourly curiosity, caught Blake's eye from the doorway. She taught economics at the college and had once, over a dropped delivery box, explained to Blake the difference between rent, which you pay to occupy, and a mortgage, which you pay toward owning, with a down payment as the entry fee. "You can't afford a down payment at your age," she'd said then, without cruelty. "Almost nobody can, straight away. So you rent, and the deposit is collateral, and you hold on to the paperwork."

He thought of that now, watching the agent amend the figure on the form. Two systems, she'd also said: one where you borrow to own and the bank takes an interest in your life for twenty-five years, and one where you pay monthly for a roof that will never be yours, and both of them want a pile of cash from you at the start. She hadn't said which was better. She'd said it depended on what else you wanted your money to do.

Blake didn't fully see it yet, that was the honest truth. He understood the cap, understood that five weeks was the ceiling and not a target, understood that the young woman was about to hand over a thousand pounds she would have to fight to get back if things went wrong. Whether renting was a trap or a rung on a ladder depended, he suspected, on things he couldn't calculate on the back of a flyer. But he could calculate this much: the difference between what was asked and what was lawful was five hundred and sixty-five pounds, and that was real money to somebody who worked at a garden centre, which the young woman had mentioned while signing.

"There's also the holding deposit," the agent said, as if offering a consolation prize. "One week's rent, capped, and it goes toward the first month if you take the place."

"Fine," the young woman said. "Five weeks, one week holding, everything in the contract, everything in writing."

"Everything in writing," the landlord agreed, and rang of keys clinked as he straightened up, a man conceding an argument one clause at a time.

Downstairs, after, Pablo bought three cans of lemonade from the corner shop and they drank them on the low wall outside. Maelys said the flat was small enough that its grandiose listing description, "a charming urban retreat," had made her laugh out loud in the hallway. Blake said he'd need to save like an asceticism, every spare pound quarantined, if he ever wanted his own place by twenty-five. Pablo said that was a noun and it didn't work like that, and Maelys said "monastic discipline, then," and Blake laughed and said fine.

Above them, on the second floor, the young woman was still inside, standing at the window of the room that might, as of the corrected paperwork, become hers. She raised her hand, once, in something between a wave and a salute, and Blake raised his can back.

activity: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
knowledge_domain: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
fact: Cindy Sherman's Untitled Film Stills (1977 to 1980) is a series of 70 black-and-white photographs of herself posed as characters from imaginary movies.
story:
Sebastian's grandmother's dining table was too big for the kitchen, so it filled the sunroom instead, its leaves propped open and its surface furred with dust that he wiped away with a dish towel before laying out his prints. Ten photographs, all of himself, all black and white, all of them somehow the same. He had taken them over three weeks: himself at the bus stop, himself reflected in the laundromat window, himself holding his father's old jacket. Laid in a row, they looked like ten copies of one boy trying on ten small moods.

The assignment had seemed easy when Mr. Haile described it. Ten artworks, one theme, plus a statement, due at the end of the month. "A portfolio is not a folder," Mr. Haile had said, walking between the desks with his hands behind his back. "It is an argument." Sebastian had liked that at the time. Now the argument appeared to be that he owned a tripod.

Sara-Maude arrived on her bicycle at four, helmet still buckled, a plastic bag of clementines swinging from one wrist. She wanted the kitchen table because her own house was being re-floored and her little brother had taken to narrating everything he did aloud, including breathing. She had her sketchbook under her arm and a plan for a comic about a lighthouse keeper who answers letters from drowned sailors. She wanted, she said, an audience for the first six pages.

She unbuckled the helmet, sat down, ate a clementine, and looked at the prints for a long moment without touching them. "They're handsome," she said, which was the kind of compliment you gave weather. "But which one is first?"

"I haven't decided. They're all kind of equal."

"That's the problem." She pulled the prints around like cards, dealing them into a new order, and stopped at the reflection one. "You know Cindy Sherman? Untitled Film Stills. It's a series of seventy black-and-white photographs, from 1977 to 1980, all of herself posed as characters from imaginary movies. Seventy." She held up the print. "You're doing kind of the opposite. Ten of one character who's real."

Sebastian had heard the name but not the work, and the shape of it snagged in him. Imaginary movies. She wasn't documenting herself; she was inventing people and casting herself in all of them. He turned the idea over while his grandmother came through with a plate of biscotti and the suspicion that neither of them had eaten anything green since Tuesday. The light in the sunroom was going amber and low, catching the dust he had failed to fully wipe away, and it occurred to him that he had been photographing his face when he should have been photographing versions of himself that had never existed. A Sebastian in a job he'd quit in his head. A Sebastian at sixty. A Sebastian his mother still imagined when he was eight.

But that felt, on second thought, like an escape. Sherman's disguises were a way of asking what a self was made of; his own plain face, repeated, might be asking the same question from the other direction, and he couldn't tell which approach was braver or whether bravery was even the right measure. What underpinned the assignment, he suspected, wasn't variety but some thread a viewer could follow from first image to last, and he still didn't know what his thread was. Pretending to be other people was one answer. Insisting on being one person was another. He sat with both, honestly unsure, and it was not an unpleasant feeling, the way standing at a fork can be pleasant if neither path is obviously wrong.

He asked his grandmother if he could photograph her wardrobe. She was an aesthete of a particular kind, suspicious of anything mass-produced, and her closet held forty years of dresses she could narrate like old friends: the one from the funeral she chose not to cry at, the one from Portugal. She carried armloads of it into the sunroom and watched him hold a scarf against his jaw in the mirror. "My affective response," she said, sipping her espresso, "is that you look like your grandfather, who was vain but beautifully so."

He set up the tripod by the window and put on the jacket again, the same jacket as the earlier print, but this time with her hat and her gloves, half her and half him, whatever that made. Sara-Maude held the reflector she'd fashioned out of tinfoil and cardboard and did not say handsome.

"Say who you are," she said, "so I know when to click."

"Her grandson," he said, "in her clothes."

"And the other nine?"

He looked through the lens at himself looking back, then reached for the cable release. "Start with this one."

activity: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
knowledge_domain: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
fact: English newspaper headlines often drop small words like 'the' and use the present tense for past events, a compressed style sometimes called 'headlinese'.
story:
The summer Ethan turned eighteen, his mother dropped him at his grandfather's house with a duffel bag, a bus ticket home dated six weeks later, and an assignment from Ms. Sutherland, his last teacher before graduation: learn to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud. She had not specified which language. The house decided that for him. Every surface held Portuguese, newspapers folded to particular columns, a radio muttering through the kitchen, his grandfather's lips moving over the crossword as if the words were beads he was counting twice.

Ethan had resisted the arrangement since April, when his mother first proposed it. He had imagined Jorge's pool, Wyatt's car with its cracked windshield, the long shapeless weeks before college. He had tried to impute motives to everyone involved, telling Jorge that his mother wanted a babysitter for the old man, telling himself that the whole thing was sentiment dressed up as education. His grandfather, for his part, asked for nothing. He set a place at the table each morning, left the paper on Ethan's chair, and waited with a patience that Ethan eventually recognized as the family stoicism, the same stillness his mother wore at funerals and hospitals.

The difficulty was immediate and humbling. On the third morning Ethan chose the shortest article he could find, four paragraphs about a tunnel project in the north, and read it aloud, halting at every third word. His grandfather corrected him without looking up from his coffee, one syllable at a time, until Ethan could feel the shape of the sentences in his mouth. Then came the summarising, which was worse. When he tried, whole clauses collapsed; he said the tunnel was old when it was new, said it ran under the river when it ran under the mountain. His grandfather laughed, a short dry sound, and slid his own paper across the table.

Ethan read the English headline and understood nothing. "Minister quits over rail delay," it said, and beneath it another, "Flood hits northern towns." He stared at the first one until the letters stopped looking like words. It seemed to have no grammar at all, no articles, verbs in the wrong tense, a minister quitting in the eternal present. His grandfather, who had been studying English at the community centre for two years, watched him struggle with something close to pleasure.

"It's wrong," Ethan said. "Where's the rest of it?"

His grandfather tapped the headline twice. "Small words gone," he said. "Is style. They call it headlinese." He took the paper back and read the line again, slower, and Ethan saw that the man was not showing off; he was guarding a piece of knowledge he had paid for, the way you guard money earned badly. His grandfather explained nothing further, so Ethan took both papers onto the porch and sat with them through the afternoon. He read the English headlines as compressed reports, present tense standing in for what had already happened, every the and of dropped for speed. Then he went back to the Portuguese article and, for the first time, read its headline the same way, as something pared down, a sentence with the fat cut off, and the first sentence of the piece made sudden sense.

That evening he summarised the article aloud at the kitchen table and got most of it right. The tunnel was subterranean, three paragraphs were about cost, one was about a woman in a village who had opposed the project for a decade. His grandfather listened with his eyes closed, which Ethan had learned was not sleep but attention. When Ethan finished, the old man was quiet for a long moment.

"She was my teacher," he said. "The woman in the village."

Ethan looked at the newspaper. The article gave her a name, an age, a quotation about the mountain, and he had flattened all of it into a summary, had turned a person into a clause. He thought of all the things he had imputed to his grandfather over the years, stubbornness, simplicity, the vague foreignness his mother hinted at when she complained about the man, and how wrong the word had been for a person who had fought a government for ten years and then closed his eyes while a stranger read about it in a new language.

He wrote to Ms. Sutherland that night, asking whether he could change his final summary to a different article, something about the tunnel itself rather than the woman. She wrote back in the morning: any article, so long as it was new to him and summarised aloud. He sat with the choice for most of the next day, rereading both pieces, weighing a kind of tidiness against a kind of truth. In the end he kept the original article, because it was harder, and because the woman's quotation, which he could now parse without a dictionary, said something he did not want to paraphrase into comfort.

On his last morning, Wyatt texted a photo of the pool, empty and glittering, and Ethan did not answer until evening. He sat on the porch with his grandfather, both papers open on the table between them, and worked through the English headlines one by one, the old man guessing at dropped words and missing tenses, Ethan correcting him now. His grandfather's memory of the woman in the village was already softening at the edges; he called her by his dead wife's name once, then again a minute later, and Ethan let it stand.

"Tomorrow you go," his grandfather said finally, folding the papers into quarters the way he always did, edges aligned, a habit of a man who had worked with his hands.

"Next summer," Ethan said, and meant it, though he could see the summer from the outside too, a whole year of college between them, Wyatt's car, Jorge's pool, the person he was still becoming somewhere his grandfather would never visit. The old man nodded once and stood, and carried both newspapers, the English one and the Portuguese one, inside stacked together under his arm.

activity: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
knowledge_domain: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
fact: Freezing food at -18 degrees Celsius (0 degrees Fahrenheit) stops bacteria from growing but does not kill most of them, so thawed food can spoil again.
story:
The week before Joshua left for college, Marlee invited him over to her house on Saturday with instructions to bring nothing except an apron if he owned one, which he did not, and a hundred dollars if he had it, which he also did not, so he brought forty and a tote bag from his mother. Rhys was already there, sitting on the counter with his phone, when Joshua came through the back door into a kitchen that smelled like onions sweating in oil. On the table lay a printed grid, seven columns, and beside it a grocery receipt annotated in Marlee's small, ferocious handwriting. "This is a week of dinners," she said, tapping the grid. "We shop once, we cook in batches today, and by tonight you'll have five meals in containers with your name on them. This is the whole skill. Everything else is improv."

Joshua had assumed cooking was the hard part. Marlee disabused him of this within ten minutes, and not gently. She walked him through the plan like a drill sergeant with a whistle in her teeth: chili on Monday and Wednesday because it held, a tray of chicken thighs and rice for Tuesday and Thursday, a pasta bake for Friday that could absorb whatever vegetables survived the week. She had already excoriated Rhys over text for proposing they buy lunch meat, so Rhys mostly kept his head down and chopped the peppers she slid toward him. When Joshua asked why they couldn't just cook whatever they felt like each night, she said, "Because 'whatever you feel like' at seven p.m. is a bag of chips and a promise, and the promise is the first thing that dies in a dorm."

They drove to the grocery store in Marlee's hatchback with the list divided three ways, and Joshua discovered that shopping was its own language. Marlee compared unit prices taped to the shelf edges, held up two bags of rice, and asked him which one the math favored, and he got it wrong twice before he got it right, and the third time she made him explain why, out loud, in the cereal aisle, while a woman with a cart waited politely to pass. Back at the house, they browned the chicken in shifts and let the chili burble on the back burner while Mr. Bighorn, the neighbor whose fence backed onto the yard, appeared at the door with a bowl of tomatoes from his garden and stayed to watch Joshua dice an onion with what he called an interesting technique. "Interesting meaning bad," Joshua said, and Mr. Bighorn said, "Interesting meaning your eyes are streaming and the onion is winning," and showed him how to keep his knuckles ahead of the blade.

It was while they were decanting the chili into containers that the trouble surfaced. Marlee's chest freezer stood in the utility room, and when she opened it to make room, Rhys went pale. At the back, buried under bags of frozen peas, sat a collection of containers that Rhys had made six weeks ago, back when he'd first attempted this same project and then abandoned it. He pulled one out and turned it in his hands like an artifact. "This was chicken curry," he said. "I made a whole batch. I figured it was fine, it's been frozen this whole time."

"Okay, but here's the thing," Marlee said, arms crossed over the container as though it might make a run for it. "Freezing food at minus eighteen degrees Celsius, which is zero Fahrenheit, which is what your freezer at school will be set to, stops bacteria from growing. It stops them. It does not kill most of them. So the second that curry comes out and thaws, everything in there that was alive before is alive again, and it starts right back up. Thawed food can spoil again, same as anything that was never frozen."

Rhys looked at the container with new suspicion. "So it's been in there with them just paused."

"Paused, not gone," Marlee said. "And you made this six weeks ago, and it sat out cooling for, what, hours?"

Rhys did not answer, which was itself an answer, and the container went into the trash bag with a sound like a small defeat. Joshua stood there holding a ladle and thinking about his own kitchen at home, the frostbitten hamburger patties his father had thawed on the counter overnight for as long as Joshua could remember, the way the meat sat there sweating all morning before anyone cooked it. He had never once thought of the freezer as anything other than a pause button that also, apparently, he had believed, sanitized. He turned the idea over the way he'd turned the unit prices over in the aisle. So the food was safe if it went in fast, stayed hard as a rock, came out and went straight into heat or the fridge, and was eaten within a day or two. The danger lived in the gaps, in the counter and the hours, not the cold itself.

"It's like they're all just waiting," he said. He meant the bacteria, and Rhys made a face, and Mr. Bighorn, from the doorway, said, "That's the spirit in which I now view my freezer as well, thank you." But Joshua kept going, because something had clicked sideways in his head. His mother had always been rigid about leftovers, three days and out, no exceptions, and he'd privately thought she was fussy, superstitious even. Now it seemed less like fussiness and more like arithmetic. At the same time, Marlee's system felt almost too engineered, five identical containers marching into Monday like a schedule that didn't know he might want to skip a night, go out with the people on his floor, let Wednesday's chili become Friday's problem. Somewhere between his mother's caution and Marlee's grid there was a version he'd have to build himself, and he couldn't build it yet, because he didn't know yet which nights he'd want free.

He wrote on masking tape with a marker, one label per container, chili with the date. His handwriting slanted and the tape wanted to curl. Rhys, who had spent the whole afternoon mispronouncing "legumes" on purpose to annoy Marlee, leaned over and read the label aloud, drawing out the word into something with four syllables and a hard g. "You say it like a normal person or I will leave you at the bus station," Marlee said, and Rhys asked how a person was supposed to know, since English spelling was a trap, and she said, "It's phonetics, there are rules, you just break all of them," which started an argument about whether "colonel" proved her point or his, an argument that was not even slightly germane to the food but that they conducted anyway, loudly, over the cooling chili.

By evening there were eleven containers stacked in Marlee's freezer, each one labeled, and the utility room smelled like cumin and dish soap. Joshua wiped down the counter and looked at the grid one more time, the seven columns with their assigned meals, and folded a copy into his tote bag next to the marker and the roll of tape. At the door, Mr. Bighorn pressed a paper bag of tomatoes into his hands and told him they'd last longer out on the counter than in the cold, and Joshua caught himself asking, "Out or in the fridge, honestly, which one?" and Mr. Bighorn smiled and said, "That depends on how fast you eat." Joshua stood on the step a moment longer, tomatoes warm against his chest, and then Marlee called from the kitchen, "Taste this before you go, I need a verdict."

activity: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
knowledge_domain: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
fact: Near the edges of real plates the field lines bulge outward and the field weakens, an effect called fringing, so E = V/d holds best near the centre.
story:
Violet's garage smelled of cut grass and old paint, and the thing on the workbench looked less like a physics apparatus than like two baking sheets having an argument. Her father had contributed the sheets, the clamps, and one strip of advice, delivered over his shoulder as he left: "Don't electrocute yourself, we need you to take the bins in." The sheets were clamped parallel, five centimetres apart, wired to a bench supply Maurice had sequestered from the school lab with a permission slip that Ms. Munro had signed without reading, which both of them felt was a kind of trust.

"Twelve volts across five centimetres," Maurice read off the multimeter, holding it like a small startled animal. "So E equals V over d. That's two thousand four hundred volts per metre." He wrote it on the concrete floor beside the bench with a piece of broken chalk, a habit from debate practice that he could not seem to shake even in a garage, as though the world were one long oratory and the floor merely a podium he had not yet mounted.

"You're getting ahead of yourself," Violet said. She had the field meter propped on a stack of paint cans, its probe held level between the plates. "The whole point is to see whether the equation is true, not to recite it and feel smug."

"It's in the textbook. Textbooks are true."

"Textbooks are true in the middle of textbook situations," Violet said, and moved the probe anyway, because she wanted the number, not the argument. Near the centre of the plates the meter read what it should, close enough that she felt a small clean click of satisfaction, the kind she never got from essays, where everything was shade and hedges. Here was a number that answered back.

Then she slid the probe toward the right edge, tracking it carefully, watching the readout. The number sagged. Not a little; it dropped by a fifth, then more, as the probe came level with the rim of the sheet. She moved it back toward the centre and watched it climb again, obedient as a plant bending toward a window.

"That's wrong," Maurice said, leaning over her shoulder. "It can't be wrong. The voltage didn't change. The distance didn't change. V over d is V over d."

"Then either the meter's broken or the universe is," Violet said, "and I know which one I'd rather blame." She swapped the probe for the school's spare, taped clumsily where Maurice had repaired it with electrical tape and optimism, and measured again. Same sag, same direction, same reluctant climb back toward the centre. She sat on an overturned bucket and stared at the plates, which stared back with the flat indifference of two baking sheets.

She had been thinking of the field as a fact, the way she'd once thought of fairness as a fact, before a semester of arguing with Maurice had sanded that down. Now she tried to picture the field as a shape, lines running from one plate to the other, straight and parallel in the middle where the world was tidy. But plates ended. Edges existed. She drew it on the chalky floor: straight lines in the centre, then, near the rim, letting them bow outward, bulging away from each other like a crowd spilling out of a doorway. If the lines bulged, they were spread thinner out there. And a field spread thinner would be weaker. E equals V over d, she thought, holds best near the centre; it is a promise the middle of the plates keeps and the edges quietly break.

"Look," she said, and Maurice crouched beside her, following her chalk lines with his finger. He was quiet for a moment, which for Maurice was a long time, like a whole minute.

"Fringing," he said. "I remember now. Ms. Munro said it once, near the end of class, when I was drawing on my arm. The lines bulge out near the edges and the field weakens. She said it fast, like it was a footnote."

"It's not a footnote, it's my entire afternoon," Violet said. "The formula isn't lying, it's just... local. It tells the truth about the middle and goes vague at the edges." She heard herself and winced, because that sounded like the beginning of one of Maurice's oratories, and she had promised herself she would keep this inchoate thing, this half-formed idea about edges, to herself until it was a real idea. But it was becoming one, right there on the concrete, in chalk.

They took five measurements across the width of the plates, and Violet graphed them on graph paper taped to the workbench, and the curve fell off at both ends exactly as her sketch had guessed, a plateau with soft cliffs. "So my lab write-up says the formula, and then it says where the formula lives," she said. "Centre, yes. Edges, no."

"Ms. Munro's going to think we're showing off," Maurice said.

"Then she should have read the permission slip." Violet packed the probe into its case, snapped it shut, and looked once more at the two baking sheets, still holding their twelve volts, still keeping their secret at the edges. "Same time Thursday," she said. "Bring better chalk."

activity: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
knowledge_domain: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
fact: In most jurisdictions traffic already on a highway has the right of way, so a merging driver must adjust speed to fit a gap rather than expect others to make room.
story:
The driving school occupied a strip mall unit between a nail salon and a tax office, and it smelled of burnt coffee and vinyl. Kate signed in at the desk, took the last seat in the back row, and listened while Ms. Foster handed out the schedule for the week. Parallel parking on Tuesday, the highway on Thursday, the test itself the following Monday. Kate had put this off for a year. Her mother called the licence a small emancipation, a way out of asking for rides to work and back, and Kate had laughed at the word, though privately she liked it. It made the whole thing sound more important than a plastic card.

Her friend Kasey had already passed, on the first try, and described the parallel parking as easy. "You just use the cones like markers," Kasey had said over the phone. "It's geometry." Kate distrusted this. Kasey described everything as easy, including the chemistry exam she had then failed. But there was something in the geometry claim that Kate kept turning over, the way she turned over a lemma in math class, a small proved thing you could stand on to reach a bigger conclusion. If parking was only a sequence of measurable moves, then it was learnable, and being learnable was different from being easy.

Tuesday arrived with light rain on the practice lot behind the building. Ms. Foster stood beside a row of orange cones in a plastic poncho, clipboard under her arm. "Pull up even with the front cone," she said. "Then turn the wheel all the way and back in slow. You'll feel it." Kate felt nothing the first three attempts. On the fourth she clipped a cone, and on the fifth she stopped six feet from the curb and sat with her hands on the wheel. "You're steering with your eyes," Ms. Foster said. "Steer with the car." Kate thought about that for a second, about how the car was a thing with a rear end that swung where she wasn't looking. She tried watching the back cone in the mirror instead of the curb ahead, and the car slid in close, maybe a foot out, but in.

"You fixed something," Ms. Foster said, and made a mark on her clipboard.

On Thursday they took the school's sedan to the ring road. Kate drove the on-ramp with her pulse loud in her ears, and Ms. Foster said, "Find your gap." Ahead on the highway a gravel truck rolled past, and beyond it a gap opened between two cars. Kate signalled and waited for the truck to shift lanes, because that was what her father did, what everyone did, and the ramp kept shrinking beneath her wheels while the truck stayed exactly where it was.

"Who has to move here?" Ms. Foster asked. "You or him?"

"Him," Kate said, and then, because the ramp was running out and the truck was not moving, she understood. "Wait. Me."

"Traffic already on the highway has the right of way," Ms. Foster said. Kate let off the brake, matched the speed of the gap behind the truck, slid into it, and merged. Her hands were shaking, but the car was in the lane, level with traffic, doing nothing wrong. She held that lane for two exits while her breathing slowed. It was a pernicious idea, she thought, that other drivers would make room, that the world would adjust itself around you. It felt entitled and it felt American and it had almost carried her onto the shoulder of a highway at ninety an hour.

She tried the merge twice more on her own judgment, and the second time a sedan in the right lane did move over, waving her in, and she lifted two fingers off the wheel in thanks while reminding herself not to expect it again. That was the confusing part. Some drivers yielded anyway, out of courtesy or boredom or pity, and you had to take the gift without building anything on it. She could hold both ideas at once, she decided, the way she held a lemma and its exceptions: the rule was the rule, and kindness happened inside the rule, never instead of it.

Back in the lot, Zacharie was waiting for his turn behind the wheel, headphones around his neck. He asked how the highway was, and Kate started to say fine, then stopped. "The truck wouldn't move over," she said. "I thought it would. It doesn't have to. You fit the gap, the gap doesn't fit you." Zacharie frowned at the phrasing, and Kasey, arriving late with an iced coffee, said, "That's what I told you. It's all geometry." Kate let it go. It wasn't all geometry. Some of it was accepting that nobody was required to make room for you, and that this was less a grievance than a fact of the road, and possibly of other roads too, the kind you walked.

The test came on a grey Monday with no rain. The examiner had a cold and a clipboard, and he directed her to a quiet street with one parked van and an ocean of space, which felt like cheating. Kate lined up even with the van, watched the back marker in the mirror, turned, eased, straightened, and came to rest eight inches from the curb. The examiner made a note and said, "Highway portion." On the ramp, a delivery truck sat in the right lane exactly where her gap wanted to be. Kate checked her mirror, found the space behind it, adjusted her speed to match, and merged into it clean, without the horn, without the swerve, without asking anyone for anything.

Afterward, in the parking lot of the strip mall, the examiner signed the paper and handed it across the seat. Kasey was leaning against the wall by the door, and Zacharie was filming her walk out for a video nobody would watch. Kate held the temporary licence up to the light, then folded it once and put it in her pocket.

"So," Kasey called. "Whose car first?"

"Yours," Kate said. "You're driving. I want to watch how you merge."

activity: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
knowledge_domain: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
fact: With typical use, about 7 in 100 people relying on the combined birth control pill for a year have an unintended pregnancy, often because doses are missed.
story:
Jeremy had volunteered to run the peer health table at the spring club fair mostly because Lyric had dared him to, and partly because his mother worked nights at a clinic and he was tired of knowing things he never said out loud. The deal was that he and Lyric would spend one lunch period a week getting trained by Mr. Nowak, then sit at a folding table in the gymnasium with pamphlets and a bowl of lollipops, answering whatever their classmates asked.

Mr. Nowak's training was quieter than Jeremy expected. He handed out cards with scenarios and made them practice out loud. "Say it in your own words," he kept saying. "If it sounds like a script, nobody hears it." Jeremy read a card about contraception aloud, stumbling only when he hit the word "intrauterine," which Lyric immediately shortened to "the T-shaped thing," and that stuck for all three of them.

The hardest card was the one about consent. Adriana, who had shown up because the club fair counted toward service hours, took it seriously in a way that surprised him. She made him rehearse the line about how consent can be withdrawn at any time, and when he mumbled it, she said, "Would you mumble it if it were about you?" He said it again, clearly, and she nodded once, like a judge.

At the clinic that Saturday, his mother let him shadow the front desk for two hours so he could learn how testing actually worked. A student from the college down the road came in for an STI panel, and Jeremy watched the receptionist explain confidentiality, the paperwork, the sliding scale. It was less dramatic than television had burnished it in his mind: no panic, no verdict, just a clipboard and a laminated sign about privacy laws.

The student asked one question on her way out. She had just been prescribed the combined pill, and she wanted to know why the nurse had been so insistent about the phone reminder, almost pushy about it. Jeremy's mother started to answer, but Jeremy got there first, because he had read the pamphlet twice in the waiting room. "With typical use, about seven in a hundred people relying on the pill for a year have an unintended pregnancy," he said, "often because doses are missed." The student looked at him, then at his mother, who raised an eyebrow and said, "He does his homework." The student set the reminder before she reached the door.

Walking home, Jeremy turned the number over. Seven felt small and enormous at the same time, depending entirely on whether you were one of the seven. He thought about how luck was capricious and how that was precisely the argument for not relying on it, though he couldn't quite make the thought land anywhere. He texted Lyric: typical use seven in a hundred, remind me to put it on a card. Lyric replied with a thumbs up and the message "the T-shaped thing rejoices."

The club fair came on a rainy Thursday, and the gym smelled of wet jackets and popcorn from the baking club next door. Their table did steady business. A sophomore asked where the nearest clinic was and how much it cost; Adriana walked her through the sliding scale without looking it up. A junior asked about condoms, and Jeremy demonstrated on a banana with such gravity that a teacher passing by laughed into her coffee. Twice, someone asked whether you could get tested without your parents finding out, and both times Jeremy gave the confidentiality speech he had memorized from the laminated sign, and both times the person's shoulders came down an inch.

Near the end, a guy from his chemistry class stopped at the table, looked around, and picked up the consent card. He read it for a long time, longer than a card takes to read. "This is about last weekend, isn't it," he said, not quite a question, and Jeremy realized he meant something Jeremy knew nothing about. He hadn't been at whatever party, hadn't seen whatever happened. All he had was the card and the sentence he had practiced until it stopped sounding like a script.

"You can take it either way," Jeremy said. "It means what it says." He held out the card, and the guy took it, folded it once, and put it in his back pocket. Then he took a lollipop, cherry by the look of the wrapper, and walked off between the popcorn table and the weightlifting club's banner, which had come loose at one corner and was swinging in the draft from the open doors.

activity: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
knowledge_domain: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
fact: Melvyn Leffler's A Preponderance of Power, which won the 1993 Bancroft Prize, argued US leaders pursued national security through dominance of the postwar world.
story:
The essay was due Monday, and Blake had brought it to his grandfather's house because the apartment he shared with his mother was too loud and the library closed at six. The prompt sat at the top of his notebook like an accusation: two historians, two explanations of the Cold War, weighed against the evidence. He had Gaddis, or the parts of Gaddis the textbook had distilled, and nothing to set against him. The grandfather's study smelled of pipe tobacco that hadn't been burned in a decade, and the desk lamp flickered when the washer downstairs ran.

"You're working," his grandfather said from the doorway, not a question. He set down a plate of sliced apples and stood reading over Blake's shoulder the way he used to read the box scores, without hurry.

"I need a second historian," Blake said. "Gaddis says the Soviets caused it, mostly. Security, spheres, Stalin as an autocrat nobody could trust. But my teacher wants me to test that against evidence, not just pick a side, and every book on the shelf says the same thing."

His grandfather pulled a chair from the corner, its feet scraping the parquet, and sat. "When I was writing my thesis," he said, "I had the opposite problem. One book and no one to argue with it. I used to argue with the radiator." He nodded toward the window. "Find your counterweight first. A good argument needs two people, otherwise it's just a man talking to a radiator."

Blake texted Daphne, who had finished her essay on Thursday because she was incapable of leaving anything unfinished. She sent back a photograph of a library catalogue entry, then a voice memo. "My dad has this huge one, Leffler, A Preponderance of Power. It won the Bancroft Prize, 1993, which my dad says is a big deal. Leffler argues American leaders pursued national security through dominance of the postwar world. Like, they thought the only safe world was one they ran." Her voice was tinny through the phone's speaker, and his grandfather raised an eyebrow but said nothing.

So that was the shape of it: Gaddis's answer and Leffler's answer, and between them the evidence Blake had been assembling all week, the Marshall Plan and the airlift and the containment doctrine and the numbers of American bases that kept growing even after the war ended. He read until the apples browned. The trouble was that the same facts seemed to fit both stories. The Marshall Plan looked like rescue under Gaddis and like a lever for dominance under Leffler, and Blake could not find any document in his stack that said, in so many words, which it was. He remembered Mr. Lin, back in tenth grade, telling the class that evidence never spoke for itself, that historians made it speak, and Blake had thought at the time this was a teacher's dodge. Now it felt more like a warning.

Charbel called at nine, wanting to complain about the swim coach, who had moved practice to six in the morning and seemed determined to inure the whole team to misery. "Anyway," Charbel said, "did you finish the Cold War thing? I just wrote that both sides were scared and called it a night."

"That's not an argument, that's a shrug."

"It's an argument if I get a B on it," Charbel said, and hung up.

Blake spread his notes across the desk. His grandfather had gone quiet in the armchair with a crossword, but Blake could feel him listening. What Blake noticed, working through the chronology again, was that Leffler's reading did not really cancel Gaddis's. Both could be true at once: the Soviets could be predatory and the Americans could be building dominance in response, and the evidence, the memoranda and the budgets, could document both without telling him which mattered more. That was the honest answer, though it was the least satisfying one, and it meant his conclusion would have to hold its own weight instead of hiding behind either historian. He thought about his grandfather, impecunious for years after the war, taking the train to interviews with one suit, and how that generation's hunger for security had a longer shadow than any of them planned. He wrote a paragraph that began, "If both explanations survive the evidence, the question becomes which explains more," and stopped, because he could hear his own uncertainty in it and could not decide whether that was weakness or honesty.

His grandfather leaned over and tapped the page with one dry finger. "When I couldn't finish a chapter," he said, "I'd read it aloud to your grandmother. She'd tell me where she stopped listening."

"Where would she stop listening to this?"

"Somewhere around 'pursued national security through dominance,'" he said. "Too many big words in a row. Then she'd ask you what it meant, and you'd better have an answer." He folded his crossword onto his knee. "Go on. Say it to me like I'm her."

Blake looked at the sentence, then at the old man waiting in the lamplight, and said, "They thought the only safe world was one they were running."

"There," his grandfather said. "Write that."

activity: ethical questions raised by technology such as algorithmic bias, surveillance and automation
knowledge_domain: ethical questions raised by technology such as algorithmic bias, surveillance and automation
fact: A 2016 ProPublica investigation found that the COMPAS risk tool misclassified Black defendants who did not reoffend as high risk at about twice the rate of white defendants.
story:
The debate topic was written on the whiteboard before anyone sat down: should algorithms decide who gets bail. Mr. Gauthier tapped the marker against the board twice and said he wanted volunteers, not hostages, and Zakk's hand went up so fast his chair scraped backward.

"Computers are neutral," Zakk said, standing. "A judge has a bad morning, holds a grudge, whatever. Code doesn't. Feed it the same facts, you get the same answer every time. That's fairer than any person."

Aidan watched from the second row, laptop open, half a search page already loaded from when Mr. Gauthier had first floated the topic on Monday. He'd meant to skim it and close the tab. He hadn't. He typed now, low against his knee, while Ashton argued the other side in a voice that kept speeding up, saying something about punishment needing a human face, about a person's freedom being too heavy a thing to hand to arithmetic.

"It's not arithmetic," Zakk said. "It's pattern recognition. It learns from data. That's the whole point."

Aidan found the article again. He'd read it twice on the bus, and the numbers had sat in him all day the way a stone sits in a shoe, small and impossible to ignore while walking. He raised his hand, and when Mr. Gauthier nodded, he didn't stand.

"So there was this tool," Aidan said. "COMPAS. Used in real courts, real bail and sentencing decisions. Journalists investigated it in 2016." He kept his eyes on the screen, then made himself look up. "Black defendants who didn't reoffend got labeled high risk at about twice the rate of white defendants who didn't reoffend."

The room had gone the particular quiet of thirty people recalculating. Zakk's mouth opened, closed.

"You're saying the algorithm was racist," he said finally.

"I'm saying what the investigation found. That's the number. Twice the rate, same direction, both groups didn't reoffend. One got called dangerous more often."

Zakk sat back down, then stood again, restless. "Okay, but that's a bad model. Somebody built it wrong. You fix the data and it's still fairer than a judge."

"Fix it with what?" Ashton said. "Data from where? All the arrests that already happened, all the sentences judges already gave?"

Aidan turned the laptop toward Zakk, who came and crouched beside the desk and read with his finger moving under the lines, which he hadn't done since maybe seventh grade. The torpid heat of the afternoon pressed against the windows and nobody moved to turn on the fans. Somewhere down the hall a class laughed at something, all at once, and stopped.

"It says here the company said it was accurate," Zakk said slowly. "Like, accurate overall."

"Overall," Aidan said. "Averaged out." He didn't finish the sentence. He let Zakk sit with the idea that an average could be true and still be unfair to someone, that the two things could happen at once, and he watched it land.

Mr. Gauthier started to speak and then visibly decided against it, writing a time on the board instead and telling them they had ten minutes to build an argument in pairs, whichever side they now actually believed in. Zakk stayed crouched by Aidan's desk a moment longer. "I still think humans are messed up," he said. "I've seen what my uncle's judges are like. But I'm not saying neutral anymore. That word's doing work it can't do."

They split the remaining time, Zakk drafting an argument for auditing the systems before deployment, which was not the position he'd held twenty minutes ago, and Aidan typing a list of questions he couldn't answer: who audits, who pays, whether a tool used on people can ever recuperate their trust once the numbers come out, whether fairness meant the same thing to the defendant and the state. At the bottom he typed one more and left it, cursor blinking after it. Did the defendant get any volition in any of this, or was he just data the moment he was booked.

The bell rang before either of them read their work aloud. Mr. Gauthier collected nothing, said only, "Same debate Thursday, new evidence welcome." Zakk snapped his notebook shut and stood in the aisle, and Aidan closed the laptop over his unanswered questions.

"You driving?" Zakk said.

"Walk."

"Then walk fast, I'll come with. I want that article on my phone before my dad starts on this at dinner."

Aidan pulled the laptop back open and turned the screen toward him.

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: Supporters of lowering the US voting age to 18 used the slogan "old enough to fight, old enough to vote," because 18-year-olds could be drafted for the Vietnam War.
story:
Laurence's cursor hovered over the "Submit registration" button for the fourth time that evening, and for the fourth time she moved it away and clicked instead on the photo of her grandmother's kitchen, the one her mother kept in the shared folder titled Cottage. The form was two fields from finished. Name, address, date of birth, and then the checkbox she had paused at: party affiliation. She had until the deadline, which was eleven days away, and she had told herself for most of those eleven days that the pause was diligence, though by now she suspected it was something closer to stage fright.

Her grandfather came through the doorway carrying two mugs, one of which he set down beside her keyboard with the handle turned toward her hand, the way he always did, as if anticipating the reach. "Still not done?" he asked. He lowered himself into the chair her mother kept by the desk for exactly this kind of visit, the one with the cushion that had gone flat from years of him.

"I can't decide about the party part," she said. "Kacey says pick one so you can vote in the primary. Daphne says independent, on principle." She rotated the mug a quarter turn without drinking from it. "They've been arguing about it since September. I think they're arguing through me at this point."

Her grandfather made a sound that was not quite a laugh. "In my family, we didn't argue. We cast the ballot my father cast, or we kept quiet about it." He looked at the screen, at the checkbox, and she watched him decide not to offer an opinion, which she understood was its own kind of courtesy. "Do you want the opinion anyway?"

"I want to know why it matters," she said. "One vote. Kacey says it doesn't, statistically, and she's the one who's read the studies. She says voting is basically a symbol, like a synecdoche, the one person standing for the whole country, and symbols don't pass laws." Kacey had actually said this at lunch with a French fry raised like a pointer, and Laurence had repeated it so many times since that it had begun to sound like her own thought, which bothered her.

Her grandfather was quiet for long enough that she looked over at him. "You know why eighteen-year-olds got the vote at all?" he asked. She shook her head. "It was the war. Eighteen-year-olds could be drafted, and the people pushing for the voting age to come down had a slogan. Old enough to fight, old enough to vote." He said it plainly, without the rise of a lesson, the way he reported the weather or the price of bread. "That was the whole argument. It fit on a sign."

Laurence turned back to the screen. She thought about the slogan, turning it over the way she turned the mug, a slow rotation. It wasn't an argument about statistics, and it wasn't a symbol either, or not only. It was a claim about fairness so parsimonious it fit on a placard: if a country could take eighteen years from you, it owed you a say in the country. Kacey's studies were about whether one vote decided anything. This was about something else, about who was allowed inside the circle the vote drew, the line it drew to circumscribe who counted. She could hold both ideas at once, she realized, the way you hold two groceries in one hand, and they did not have to agree. She still didn't know if her vote would matter. She knew now why she wanted to cast it anyway.

"Grandpa," she said. "When you turned eighteen, were you drafted?" He was already shaking his head before she finished. "Canada," he said. "Lucky timing, and a father with a deferment I never asked about. My brother wasn't lucky, though he came home." He picked up his mug and drank from it slowly. "I voted the first chance they gave me. Never missed one since. Not because I thought it decided things. Because somebody had carried that sign for me before I was born."

Laurence moved the cursor back to the form. She left the party affiliation blank for now, the independent box unchecked too, because that was a decision she could make tomorrow with Daphne's and Kacey's messages still open in front of her, and tonight was for the rest of it. She typed her date of birth, checked it twice, and pressed Submit. The confirmation page bloomed pale green, and beside her, her grandfather set down his mug and reached over to tap the desk once, twice, like applause in miniature.

"There," he said. "Now you're the dangerous kind of citizen."

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: A violin's four strings are tuned in perfect fifths to G, D, A and E, from lowest to highest.
story:
The violin felt like an animal that hadn't decided whether to trust him. Michael had signed up for the strings elective on a whim in September, and by October he could still barely draw the bow across without a sound like a dying seagull. He stayed after class in the music room on Tuesdays, when Ms. Nguyen left the practice rooms open and the late sun came through the blinds in long bars across the carpet. Today he was trying to tune the thing, which meant turning four little pegs and hoping.

Kylie was in the next practice room over, and she was arguing with her own violin. He could hear her plucking one string, then another, then groaning. "Which one is which," she said through the door, not really a question, more a complaint aimed at the universe. She came out holding the instrument like it had betrayed her. "I keep playing a D on the A string and then wondering why everything sounds haunted."

"You could just remember them," Michael said. He meant it kindly, but she gave him a look.

"I can't remember anything I can't sing." She plucked the fattest string, the one nearest her chin when she held the instrument properly. "There's a trick, though. Guneet told me. You go from the fattest one, the lowest, up to the thinnest, the highest, and it's G, D, A, E." She plucked each one in turn, and Michael leaned in to listen. "G, D, A, E, lowest to highest. She said they're tuned in perfect fifths, whatever that means. Good Dogs Always Eat, she said, and now that's stuck in my head forever, so at least something is."

Michael took his own violin and plucked the fat string, then the next one, then the next. G, then D, then A, then E, each one a little brighter, a little thinner under his finger. He hummed the G and then the D and noticed, with a small jolt of curiosity, that they sounded somehow related, like two versions of the same idea. Fifths. He didn't know why that word, or what made a fifth perfect, and he liked not knowing; it felt like a door he could come back to. "Good Dogs Always Eat," he repeated, and Kylie said, "See, it's already got you."

At home that night he wrote an email to Guneet, who had moved to Halifax in August and still wrote back like she was leaving notes in his locker. He typed: "Your string trick works. I got through a whole piece without sounding haunted. But here's my question. When I pluck G and then D one after the other, they sound like they agree about something. Do you hear that too, or am I inventing it? Also I'm sorry I said your mnemonic was babyish when we were eleven. In my defense, I was extremely eleven." He read it over, deleted "extremely," put it back, and hit send.

The reply came the next morning, and he read it on the bus with his violin case wedged between his knees. "Of course they agree, they're fifths, that's the whole point, Michael. But I'm not going to pontificate about music theory at you because you'd fall asleep and drool on the bus, I know you're reading this on the bus. Go pluck them and listen harder. Also, accepted apology. You were a pugnacious eleven-year-old. You once fought a chair."

In the practice room on Tuesday, Ms. Nguyen stopped in the doorway and listened while Michael tuned, plucking G, then D, then A, then E, adjusting the pegs in tiny increments until the pairs of notes sat next to each other in his ear like they belonged together. "You're hearing it," she said, which was all she said, and Michael wondered how she could tell from across the room, whether agreement between notes is something you can hear in someone's shoulders.

He had wanted, all autumn, to sound like the recordings, clean and confident. Now he found he wanted something smaller and stranger: to keep noticing the way G leaned toward D, the way the order of the strings made a kind of staircase you could climb with your fingers. Maybe that was the same impulse that made people argue about which bands mattered, the whole zeitgeist thing Guneet was always going on about, everyone hunting for the pattern underneath the noise. He didn't know. He put the bow on the D string, breathed, and drew it across.

From the next room, Kylie knocked twice on the wall, their signal for "that one sounded alive." Michael knocked back once, meaning wait, and played it again.

activity: terms related to responsibility, trade-offs and unintended consequences used in structured ethical reasoning
knowledge_domain: terms related to responsibility, trade-offs and unintended consequences used in structured ethical reasoning
fact: In 1902, French colonial authorities in Hanoi paid a bounty for each rat tail, and people began cutting off tails and releasing the rats to breed, so the rat problem grew.
story:
Mr. Otieno set the chalk down and wrote a single word on the board: *incen?* He left it half-finished, which Kayla found more dramatic than he probably intended. The question on the table, taken from a real proposal circulating among the student council, was whether the school should pay students five dollars for every instance of vandalism they reported. Kayla had written the proposal. Only Katarina knew that, and Katarina had promised, with the solemnity of someone swearing on a grave, to keep it quiet until the vote on Friday.

"Paying people to do the right thing works," Kayla said, leaning forward over the seminar table. "It's not cynical, it's realistic. You want more of a behavior, you reward it. Every econ teacher in this building would back me."

Julianne turned her pen over and over against the desk, a small clatter that seemed interminable in the pause that followed. "So the kid who was going to smash a window anyway now gets paid to snitch on someone else who does. And the kid who reports the most wins some invisible competition. What exactly are we rewarding, Kayla? Reporting, or honesty?"

"Reporting," Kayla said. "Honesty is what we hope reporting produces." She heard the distinction wobble as she said it, like a chair with one short leg, but she pushed on, because the vote was Friday and because thirty-two of the forty signatures on the petition had come from her own lunch period, gathered in two days of her telling people the plan was airtight.

Mr. Otieno, who had been standing by the window with his arms folded, asked his usual question, the one he asked about everything. "And if it works too well? What does the world look like if everyone obeys you perfectly?" He said it mildly, as though he were asking about the weather, and walked back toward the board to finish the word he had started.

That was when Katarina looked at Kayla across the table, and Kayla understood that her friend was about to break the grave-swearing promise, or worse, was waiting for Kayla to break it herself. Katarina knew the other thing. The thing from Sunday dinner.

Because on Sunday, Kayla had proposed to her mother that her little brother be paid per chore, two dollars each, chore defined as whatever got checked off the list on the refrigerator. Her mother had looked at her for a long moment over the roast, and then, instead of arguing, had told a story. In 1902, French colonial authorities in Hanoi paid a bounty for each rat tail. People began cutting off the tails and releasing the rats to breed. The rat problem grew.

"That's disgusting," her brother had said, delighted.

"That's an incentive," her mother had said, and passed the potatoes.

Kayla had thought about it for exactly one day, and then she had decided it didn't apply. Rats were rats. Teenagers were not rats. A school was not a colony, and reporting vandalism was not breeding rats in a basement and selling their tails while the animals themselves went on living, multiplying, chewing through the walls. She had almost convinced herself. She had gotten forty signatures in a state of near conviction.

"It can backfire," Katarina said now, quietly, into the silence Mr. Otieno had left standing in the room. "Things you pay for can backfire in ways you didn't plan. Like the rats."

A few people laughed, because they assumed Katarina was being random. Julianne didn't laugh. "What rats?"

Kayla's mouth was dry. She could deflect, let Katarina explain, let the class malign her friend as the one with the weird animal facts, and keep her own authority intact for the Friday vote. Or she could do the other thing. Mr. Otieno was watching her with the patient, unhurried attention of a man who had watched a lot of people arrive at this exact fork and was interested to see which road each of them took.

"Hanoi, 1902," Kayla said. "The French colonial authorities paid a bounty for each rat tail. So people started cutting off the tails and releasing the rats to breed. The rat problem grew." She let that sit, the way her mother had let it sit over the roast. "I proposed paying my brother per chore on Sunday. My mom told me that. And I wrote this proposal on Monday anyway, because I decided it was different. I'm not sure it's different."

"So what do we do," Julianne said, and it wasn't a attack anymore; the question came out slower, genuinely puzzled. "Never reward anything? Just hope people do right for free?"

"Maybe there's a trade-off," Kayla said. "You give up some control over what you're actually buying. That's the cost. Maybe sometimes it's still worth paying, and maybe sometimes you're buying tails while the rats walk out the door. I don't have a rule that tells you which time is which."

Mr. Otieno finished the word on the board. *incentive*, and under it, in smaller letters, *perverse incentive*, and under that, *unintended consequences*. He tapped the chalk twice against the last phrase and looked at Kayla.

"You could have let Katarina take the hit," he said.

"I know," Kayla said. She looked down at her notebook, at her own handwriting, the bullet points she had prepared, the phrase she had underlined twice: *the plan is airtight*. She drew a single line through it, all the way across.

"Vote's Friday," Katarina said, and nudged the petition sheet across the table toward her. "Thirty-two signatures, still yours."

Kayla picked up her pen.

activity: the idea of opportunity cost, that choosing one thing means giving up the next best alternative
knowledge_domain: the idea of opportunity cost, that choosing one thing means giving up the next best alternative
fact: Opportunity cost counts only the single next-best alternative given up, not all the alternatives added together.
story:
The application deadline was Sunday at midnight, and the store needed someone for both weekend shifts, and Maika sat on her bedroom floor with her back against the bed because sitting at the desk made the choice feel too official. The portfolio had to be submitted with a fee of forty dollars she did not have. Two shifts paid sixty. She had already texted the manager to ask which days, and the manager had written back that she could take Saturday only, Sunday only, or both, her choice.

Hailee called at nine. "Are you coming Saturday? Malaya's driving, we're leaving at four."

"I might have to work."

"You said the portfolio was due Sunday. You can do the trip and the portfolio."

"Not the money part." Maika looked at the crumpled schedule on her quilt, where she had written out the weekend in columns. Saturday: shift, nine to six. Trip to the city with Hailee and Malaya, four to eleven. Sunday: shift, ten to four. Portfolio submission, all day. Ms. Carvalho's open studio hours, one to three, where she had promised to look over final images with anyone who came.

"So skip Sunday's shift," Hailee said.

"If I skip Sunday I can go to Ms. Carvalho's. If I skip Saturday I can come with you. If I skip both I have nothing." Maika flattened the paper against her knee. "I keep adding it up. Both shifts is sixty, one is thirty, and if I don't come Saturday I lose the trip, and if I skip Ms. Carvalho's I lose her looking at my stuff before I send it. It's like I'm giving up a hundred and fifty things at once."

There was a pause on the line, and then Malaya's voice, closer, as if Hailee had put her on speaker in the car. "You're doing the thing Ms. Carvalho talked about in the econ unit. You can't add all of it up. It's just the one thing."

"What one thing?"

"The next best thing. Whatever you'd actually do if you weren't working. Not everything stacked." Malaya sounded like she was eating something. "She called it opportunity cost. It only counts the single next-best alternative, not all of them added together."

Maika pulled her knees up. On the paper, in her own handwriting, she had drawn a bracket around Saturday's shift and the trip, and another around Sunday's shift and the studio hours, and the brackets looked like fences that circumscribed the whole weekend, as if the days were already smaller than they were. "So if I work Saturday, what I lose is the trip. Just the trip."

"Whichever one you'd pick if you weren't working. That's the only one that counts."

"That seems too easy."

"It seems too small," Malaya said. "It is small. That's the point. Everything else you're not doing doesn't count."

After they hung up, Maika laid the schedule on the bed and stood over it. She had written a turgid paragraph in her application essay about sacrifice, three sentences of it, and reading it now she felt her ears go warm; it was the kind of writing that promised grandeur and delivered nothing, a small collapse she could not undo before Sunday. The trip with Hailee and Malaya would be loud and long and she would come home tired. Ms. Carvalho's studio hours would be quiet, and Ms. Carvalho would point at two photographs and say one thing about each, and that one thing would be true.

She texted the manager: Saturday only. Then she texted Ms. Carvalho: Can I come Sunday at one?

The reply came while she was taping the schedule back above her desk. "I'll be there till three. Bring the prints, not the laptop."

Maika took the essay off her screen and read the sacrifice paragraph again. She could cut it, and the essay would be shorter and plain, or she could leave it and the page would stay full. She highlighted the three sentences and sat with her finger on the delete key, and outside her window a car door slammed somewhere down the street, twice, like someone loading something heavy.

She deleted the paragraph and started typing. On Saturday she would stand at the register for nine hours and miss the highway and Malaya's playlist and whatever Hailee had planned that she hadn't said out loud. On Sunday she would carry her prints up to the studio at one o'clock.

At eleven, Hailee sent a photo from the car, the dashboard lit up, Malaya's hand in the frame holding a gas station receipt. Maika set her alarm for seven-thirty, laid out her work shirt on the chair, and turned off the lamp. "Next best thing," she said to the ceiling, and put the phone face down on the nightstand.

activity: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
knowledge_domain: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
fact: The principle called Chekhov's gun, from the playwright Anton Chekhov, holds that anything clearly shown on stage early should matter later in the play.
story:
Matthew signed up for drama in September because it filled the last slot on his timetable and because Mr. Singh had a reputation for not assigning essays. The first real assignment was announced on a Tuesday: a ten-minute play, staged before the class in November, drawn from a moment in the playwright's own life. Matthew wrote his in one sitting in the school library, four pages about the night his father moved out, when he was eleven, and about the letter his father left on the kitchen counter, which nobody in the family had ever opened.

At the table read, six classmates sat around the props room with photocopies while Calla, who had the mother's part, followed the pages with a pencil. The letter appeared in the first scene, described in a stage direction as sitting by the fruit bowl, and then it was never mentioned again. The play ended with the boy watching the taillights go and turning off the porch light.

"Where does the letter come back?" Matthias asked. He was reading the father's part and kept his pencil on the page like a bookmark. "It's right there in scene one, and then it just sits there for nine minutes. Why is it there?"

"You can't just have something onstage that never matters," Calla said, not looking up from her pencil marks. "There's a principle. Chekhov's gun. Anton Chekhov, the playwright. Anything clearly shown on stage early should matter later in the play." She shrugged. "We did him in English last year."

Mr. Singh, who had been listening from the doorway with his coffee, said only, "Take it up with your writer," and left them to it.

Matthew said the letter was real, that it actually existed, still sealed, in a drawer at his mother's apartment, and that life did not tidy itself into setups and payoffs. Matthias said that was fine for life but this was a stage, four metres by three, where everything the audience could see was a choice. Matthew called him doctrinaire, said a rule about guns did not obligate every envelope. Matthias said, "Then don't put the envelope where I can see it." Calla, who was supposed to be memorizing antigen diagrams for biology, said the immune system had the same problem, deciding what was self and what was foreign, and that a stage was like that too, everything out there either belonging or not. Nobody thanked her for the comparison.

Matthew went home on the late bus and opened the drawer. The envelope had yellowed slightly at the fold. He did not open it. He sat on the floor of his mother's apartment for a while with it in his hands, and he understood something that he did not yet have words for: that keeping the letter onstage and unopened was not sloppiness, it was the whole point, but only if the play knew that, only if the audience was made to feel the weight of the thing that never happens.

He rewrote the ending over two nights. The boy still turned off the porch light, but now he came back inside, picked up the letter, carried it to his room, and put it in a drawer that he left open a hand's width so the audience could see the envelope sitting inside. Nothing exploded. Nobody read anything aloud. The mother came in, asked what he was doing, and he said, "Nothing," and closed the drawer, and the lights went down on the closed drawer.

On performance day, the class sat in the black box in a rough semicircle. Matthias played the father with his jacket already on. Calla played the mother with her biology notes still folded in her back pocket.
