The letter was a blank envelope Matthew had brought from home, not the real one, though at the dress rehearsal he had caught himself half convinced the prop was somehow the original, as if staging the moment could reify it, make the sealed drawer into the drawer, the play's fake November into the real one from five years ago.

The performance ran nine minutes and forty seconds. There was a small silence at the end, the good kind, and then Mr. Singh asked for comments. A girl from the third row, who had said nothing all term, raised her hand. "So what was in the letter?"

Matthew looked at the drawer, which was still closed on the empty envelope. "I don't know," he said. "I've never opened it."

"Are you going to?"

He picked up the prop envelope from the drawer and turned it over once in his hands. "Ask me after the next draft."

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: The GED tests were created in 1942 to let military service members and veterans who had not finished high school show high-school-level skills.
story:
The paper napkins had been folded into fans, which Brayden took as a bad sign, though he couldn't have said why. His grandmother did that only when she wanted a dinner to look like something, and a dinner that needed to look like something usually had a speech in it. He sat between his cousin and the empty chair reserved for his grandfather, who was parking the truck.

"You're the graduate," his grandfather said, arriving at last and taking the chair. "So what'd they teach you at that school. Anything worth the property tax."

"Photosynthesis," Brayden said. "Some French."

His grandfather grunted and reached for the bread. This was the routine. Brayden had spent four years assembling a transcript that his grandfather treated as a receipt for services not rendered, and tonight, of all nights, the routine had begun early.

The problem was the toast. His mother had cornered Brayden in the kitchen an hour before and told him he would say something, that his grandfather had driven three hours, that after the insolvency scare two winters ago the family didn't take dinners like this for granted, and that Brayden would find something kind to say. Brayden had said fine. He had meant it, mostly. But he couldn't get past the feeling that anything he praised about school, the diploma, the ceremony in the hot gym with Lincoln's family on one side and Aaryan's on the other, his grandfather would hear as a small insult to the life he'd lived without any of it. And Brayden didn't want to give the toast like an apology, either, because that would be worse, an insult wearing manners.

Between the salad and the main course, Aaryan texted him a photo from the ceremony, Brayden mid-shuffle across the stage, and Brayden laughed before he could stop himself. His grandfather asked what was funny. Brayden passed the phone across the table.

"That your friend," his grandfather said. "The one who's going to be a doctor."

"Aaryan. Maybe. First he's going to be a college freshman who eats a lot of dining hall pasta."

His grandfather turned the phone over in his hands the way he handled remotes, as though it might be booby-trapped. "You know I didn't do that," he said. "The stage, the hat. I enlisted at seventeen."

Brayden had heard this before, but always as a complaint about modern softness, never as a fact with edges. "So what happened after," he said. "The service."

" after the service." His grandfather put down the fork. "They made a test. Nineteen forty-two. For fellows like me, service members and veterans who hadn't finished high school. You took it and it showed you had the skills anyway. That's how they did it. I got mine in fifty-one, in a storefront in Toledo." He said this flatly, without pride and without shame, the way he reported crop prices.

Brayden sat with that. His whole life the GED had been a word teachers used as a warning, the thing you'd end up with if you kept skipping. And here it was on his grandfather's side of the table, older than his grandmother, invented for men in uniform. He tried to hold both ideas at once and found they wouldn't sit still. Maybe the test had always meant two different things depending on which side of it you were standing, and maybe his jaundiced view of it, inherited from hallways and guidance counselors, said more about the hallways than the test.

The toast arrived with dessert. His mother looked at him. Brayden stood, tapped his glass, and felt every fan-folded napkin in the room turn toward him.

"I used to think the diploma was the point," he said. "It's a piece of paper with my name spelled right, which is not nothing." A few laughs. "But there's more than one way to prove you know something. Grandpa did it in a storefront in Toledo. I did it in a gym that smelled like floor wax. I don't know yet which way matters more, or whether they're the same thing wearing different hats. But I'm glad we're both at this table." He lifted his glass. "To proving it however you have to."

His grandfather didn't smile, exactly, but he raised his water glass a half inch and held it there a moment longer than the others.

Later, when the plates were stacked and the cousins were arguing about card games, his grandfather caught Brayden by the kitchen door. "That was all right," he said. Then he added, almost too quietly, "They still let old fellows take it, you know. In case you ever wondered." He pressed something small into Brayden's hand. It was a worn paper card, creased twice, with a seal in the corner and a date from before either of Brayden's parents was born.

activity: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
knowledge_domain: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
fact: Making ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen is exothermic, so low temperatures favour more ammonia at equilibrium, but industrial plants run hotter because the reaction is too slow when cold.
story:
The room smelled of burnt coffee from the lab tech's corner kettle, and Katherine had claimed the stool by the window because it was the only one that didn't wobble. Ms. Flores had written one problem on the board and then left the room, which was her version of trust. Nitrogen plus hydrogen gives ammonia, forward reaction exothermic. Predict the effect of increasing the temperature.

Charlene leaned over from the next station. "It shifts left. Away from ammonia. Cold favours it, so hot unfavours it." She said it the way she said most things, as though the universe had been sorted into columns this morning and she had the clipboard.

"Which means," Katherine said, "if you wanted to make a lot of ammonia, you'd run the plant as cold as you could get away with."

"Obviously."

Maelle, who had been morose since the cross-country coach cut her from the relay, looked up from a notebook she'd been decorating with a border of small doomed fish. "Then why does my dad say the plant where he works runs hot? He's a shift supervisor. He complains about the heat every single dinner."

Charlene waved this off. "Your dad probably runs a different part. Or he's exaggerating. Adults exaggerate about work. It's like a union rule."

Katherine wrote both claims in her notebook, side by side, and then sat looking at them. The equilibrium argument was clean. If the reaction gave off heat, then adding heat pushed it backward, the way pushing on one side of a seesaw lifts the other. Cold in, more ammonia out. That part she trusted, partly because she'd derived it and partly because Ms. Flores had made them chant the principle until the class sounded like a cult with a midterm. But Maelle's father was a real person in a real building full of pipes, and real buildings had a way of problematizing tidy rules. She had learned this the previous semester in civics, when a perfectly logical argument about voting had collided with an actual schedule.

"Can we call him?" Katherine asked.

"It's eleven in the morning."

"He's on shift. He's bored. Supervisors love explaining things, it makes them feel supervisory."

Maelle texted. For four minutes nobody said anything, and Charlene restacked the graduated cylinders that were already stacked. Then the phone buzzed, and Maelle read aloud: "He says yeah, cold makes more ammonia at equilibrium, quote, that part you got right. But they run it hotter anyway. Cold, the reaction basically just stands there. Too slow. You'd get a purer result about once a month. Hot gives less ammonia each pass but gives it now."

Katherine copied this down under the first column. So both things were true. Low temperature favoured more ammonia at equilibrium; the plants ran hotter because the reaction was too slow when cold. It was not a contradiction so much as a negotiation, the kind where neither side gets everything and the accountant decides. Equilibrium told you where you'd end up if you waited forever. The plant did not have forever. It had shareholders.

"Ms. Flores lied to us," Charlene said, but without conviction.

"She didn't lie. She just didn't finish." Katherine drew a bracket around both columns and wrote a question mark next to it, because that was the honest part. She could hold the two ideas together, could even explain them to Maelle, who was now drawing her fish larger and more hopeful. What she couldn't do was say where the ideal temperature actually was, or who had found it, or whether it changed when the price of ammonia changed. That stayed dark. She underlined the question mark twice, which was as close as her notebook got to shrugging.

Ms. Flores came back with a sandwich and read the board. "You've reached the good part," she said. "The exam stops at the principle. The plant doesn't." She pointed her sandwich at Katherine's bracket. "Nice mark. What is it?"

"A thing I don't know yet."

"Keep it," Ms. Flores said. "Most people erase those."

The bell rang. Charlene gathered her things and paused at the door, and Katherine could see her rearranging the universe into columns again, this time with a third column she didn't like. "So the right answer on the test," Charlene said, "is the wrong answer in the factory."

Maelle zipped her bag. "My dad says the fish tank in the break room has a really good substrate. He says that about everything, though."

"He means the gravel," Katherine said. "Probably."

"Katherine." Charlene stood in the doorway, holding it open with one hip, patient as a person who has just discovered the world is graded on a curve she can't see. "If I write what's true on the test, do I pass?"

Ms. Flores, from behind her sandwich, said, "Which true?"

activity: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
knowledge_domain: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
fact: Arabic newspapers across many countries are written in Modern Standard Arabic rather than local spoken dialects, so one written form serves readers in different regions.
story:
The newspaper arrived at his grandfather's house every Thursday, wrapped in brown paper and smelling faintly of ink and the long journey it had made. Alexis had spent three summers here, in the rooms with their tiled floors and the lemon tree in the courtyard, and in all that time the paper had sat folded on the table like furniture. Now it was his assignment, and he was afraid of it.

"The article on page five," his grandfather had said that morning, tapping the newsprint with one crooked finger. "You will read it to me after lunch, and you will tell me what it says. In Arabic, out loud, in your own words." He had not explained why, and Alexis had not asked, because his grandfather never assigned anything without a reason, and because the reason always announced itself eventually, on its own schedule.

Alexis spread the paper on the kitchen table and began to read. The first sentence stopped him like a locked gate. He knew the letters; he could sound out every word, laboriously, the way he had once sounded out English in the first grade. But the words were wrong. Not unknown, exactly. Warped. The Arabic he knew came from his grandfather's mouth, from the kitchen and the courtyard and the long phone calls to relatives, and it ran quick and idiomatic and full of shortcuts. This Arabic stood stiffly at attention, wore unfamiliar endings, refused every abbreviation he knew. He read the headline four times and it remained equivocal, hovering between two possible meanings, and he could not decide which.

He called Arian, whose parents had come from Casablanca and whose house smelled of different spices but held the same kind of grandmother-driven chaos. "Can you read your parents' paper?" Alexis asked. "The Arabic one."

"Sure," Arian said. "Badly. My dad laughs at me. Why?"

"Does it sound like how your dad talks? Like actually how he talks?"

There was a pause, the sound of Arian considering. "No. Not even close. It's like, formal. He says nobody talks like that." Arian's voice dropped as if sharing a secret. "But he reads it fine. So does my uncle in Marseille, and he's from a whole different generation."

Alexis sat with that. His grandfather spoke one way, Arian's father another, and yet both men read this same written language without complaint. The paper on the table had been printed in Cairo; Arian's came from somewhere else entirely; the differences between the two households, when they spoke, were wide enough that Alexis sometimes caught only fragments of Arian's father's rapid-fire sentences. Yet here was a single written form bridging all of it, one printed Arabic that belonged to no one's tongue and everyone's page.

After lunch his grandfather settled into his chair by the window and waited. Alexis stood with the paper and read the article aloud, haltingly, his voice thin. The stiffness that had blocked him on the page loosened slightly in his mouth; some of the formal words, once spoken, revealed cousins among the words he knew, and he grabbed at those connections. When he finished reading, he closed his eyes and tried to summarize.

"It is about the water," he began. "In the, the villages along the river. The ones in the south." He heard his own dialect leaking through, the comfortable shapes his grandfather had inured him to over years of kitchen conversations, and he watched the old man's face for a verdict. "The article says the villages need... help. That people are waiting."

His grandfather nodded once, slowly. "Good. Now again, and slower."

On the second telling, the words came steadier, and Alexis noticed his grandfather's eyes had gone somewhere far past the window. That was when Alexis finally asked. "Why this article? Why today?"

His grandfather was quiet long enough that the courtyard clock ticked through a full minute. "The river in the article," he said at last. "Your grandmother was born near it. Sixty years she has told me stories about that water, and now it is in the news, and she is in the hospital, and I cannot sit there every hour." He looked at Alexis directly. "When she comes home, she will want to know what the papers are saying. Her eyes are not good enough to read them. Yours will have to be."

Alexis looked down at the newsprint, at the formal sentences that had resisted him all morning. He understood now why his grandfather had chosen the slow way, the assignment, the repetition: he was being prepared for a duty he had not known existed. He thought, too, of something Mr. Cohen, the retired teacher next door, had once said when Alexis had complained that there was no single right way to translate a phrase, that every version gave up something. Mr. Cohen had called that relativism with real approval, as if it were a liberation rather than a loss. Alexis had liked the sound of it then. Now, holding a newspaper his grandmother would depend on him to voice, he was less sure. Some renderings were plainly better than others, and the difference mattered, and he could not pretend otherwise.

"What I told you," he said to his grandfather, "was it right? The summary. Was it true to the article?"

His grandfather considered him. "Mostly true. A little wrong in the middle, where you guessed. Tomorrow you will read it again and find the parts you smoothed over." He picked up the paper himself, ran his thumb along the column, and handed it back. "It is called Modern Standard Arabic, what is written there. It is not how anyone talks. But it is how everyone reads." He folded his hands. "Again. From the beginning."

Alexis took a breath, set his finger under the first line, and began.

activity: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
knowledge_domain: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
fact: In the United States, a conventional mortgage with a down payment below 20 percent usually requires private mortgage insurance, which protects the lender, not the buyer.
story:
The bank smelled like carpet cleaner and cold air, and Lily counted the money in her head again while she stood in line. Forty-one hundred dollars. She had counted it twice on the bus, once folded into the deposit slip her grandmother had printed at the library, and the number had come out the same each time, but she counted again anyway, because today the number had to be right. Behind the teller's window a man in a gray suit was explaining something to a young couple, and Lily could hear only fragments: escrow, principal, the word amortized drifting over the velvet rope like a rumor.

Her grandmother stood beside her holding a folder of papers against her coat. "It's a condo on Fell Street," she had told Lily last week, over rice and beans. "Two bedrooms, and the seller would take one sixty-two." Lily had nodded as though this were an ordinary thing, her grandmother buying a place at seventy-one, after thirty years in other people's houses, and then had gone home and lain awake doing arithmetic on her phone until the screen dimmed on its own.

The teller took the envelope and the slip, and Lily watched her count, watched her fingers move without hurry. This was the part she had been afraid of, the space between handing it over and finding out whether the money she had earned at the garden center for two summers, plus the babysitting, plus what Bently's mother had paid her for designing a poster for the bakery, was enough. The teller stamped the deposit. "Forty-one hundred even," she said, and slid the receipt across the marble.

They were shown into a small office where a loan officer named on the desk plaque only as a branch associate spread out her grandmother's papers. Lily sat with her hands under the table. The woman talked through the price, the loan amount, the interest rate, and then she said, "With a down payment of ten percent, you'd be looking at private mortgage insurance as well." Lily's grandmother sat very still. "My cousin's mortgage had a charge like that," she said. "Private mortgage insurance. It protects the lender, not the buyer." The woman nodded and moved on to closing costs, but Lily had stopped moving entirely, because she remembered something.

She remembered her grandfather, the year before he died, sitting at the kitchen table with the older cousin's paperwork spread in front of him, explaining over his coffee why there was an extra charge on the monthly statement. Lily had been fourteen and had not cared; she had been texting Bently about a history exam, a question about how to historicize the New Deal, whether you could understand it at all outside the desperation that made it. Her grandfather had tapped the paper and said the cousin had put down too little, and there was a price for that, and Lily had looked up just long enough to see the number he was pointing at. She had forgotten it until now, and now she could not unknow it.

She did the arithmetic on the loan officer's offered notepad while the woman kept talking. Twenty percent of one sixty-two was thirty-two thousand four hundred. Her grandmother had the eleven thousand from the sale of the old furniture and the small insurance leftover, plus Lily's forty-one hundred, plus six thousand in a certificate of deposit maturing in March. Lily added it three times. Twenty-one thousand, and change. Short by more than ten thousand, and every month until they reached twenty percent, the insurance charge would ride along on top of the interest, on top of the taxes, money paid out that bought them nothing.

"May I ask a question?" Lily said, and her voice came out steadier than she expected. "If we waited, and saved until the down payment was twenty percent, then there'd be no private mortgage insurance at all?" The officer's answer was equivocal, something about how rates change and markets change and nothing could be guaranteed, but the shape of the answer underneath the hedging was yes. Lily looked at her grandmother, who was looking at the notepad, at the column of figures in a teenager's handwriting, and Lily understood that her grandmother had known all along that they were short, had known before they walked in, and had brought Lily's deposit to the bank anyway so that Lily would see the whole picture rather than be told about it. Her grandfather had done the same thing once, showing the cousin's statement instead of lecturing. Their family did not explain. They let you stand in front of the thing.

Her grandmother said, quietly, "The apartment will still be there in the spring, maybe. Or another one." Lily thought of her government class, the teacher droning about what a polity owes its renters and its owners, and how she had written an essay arguing that ownership was everything, and how the essay had not once considered what it cost to arrive at twenty percent. She did not have a settled position anymore. Maybe the insurance charge was bearable if it meant her grandmother stopped hauling laundry to the basement of a building where the landlord raised the rent every September like clockwork. Maybe waiting a year was the disciplined path and the year would cost her grandmother something no spreadsheet could show. Both were true at once, and the loan officer's neatly printed sheet did not have a column for that.

They declined the application for now, gathered the folder, and walked out through the carpeted hush. At the door her grandmother took Lily's arm, more for steadiness than for warmth, and said, "In the spring, you'll come with me again, and this time we'll bring the whole twenty percent." Outside, the bus pulled up to the corner in a wash of diesel, and Lily reached into her pocket and closed her hand around the deposit receipt.

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: In a 1999 study, Tanya Chartrand and John Bargh found that people liked a partner more when that partner quietly mimicked their posture and gestures, even without noticing the mimicry.
story:
Florence arrived at the park eleven minutes early, which she decided to think of as eight minutes early plus three minutes of sitting on a bench getting her face under control. The date was with a boy from her chemistry class, and they had agreed, in the flat language of text messages, to meet by the fountain at two. She had dressed carefully and then undressed carefully twice, and now she wore the third option, a green jacket she did not entirely trust.

Jayna and Heaven had appointed themselves her advisors, which mostly meant they had opinions. "You're overthinking," Jayna had said at lunch, while Heaven shook her head with the slow certainty of someone adjudicating a dispute she had already decided. "She's not overthinking, she's preparing. There's a difference." Florence had let them argue because it was easier than admitting she did not know which of them she agreed with.

The boy arrived at two exactly, holding two cans of soda from the machine near the tennis courts, one of which was the kind she had once mentioned liking, a detail she was surprised he had kept. They walked the gravel loop around the duck pond, and the conversation went the way first conversations go, in questions that were really small doors: favorite teachers, worst field trips, whether the new library carpet was deleterious to public health or merely ugly. He made her laugh about the carpet. She noticed that she was doing most of the laughing and tried to slow it down, then forgot to.

Near the third bench they sat, and it happened that both of them leaned forward on their elbows at the same moment, forearms on knees, chins more or less in hands, so that if someone had photographed them from behind they would have looked like mirror halves. Florence noticed this the way you notice weather. Then she remembered where she had learned about it.

Mr. Tse had included it in a unit on social psychology, a slide she had copied down mostly because his tests rewarded copying. In 1999, two researchers, Tanya Chartrand and John Bargh, did a study where a partner in a conversation quietly mimicked a person's posture and gestures, and afterward the person liked that partner more, without noticing the mimicry at all. She had written it, been tested on it, forgotten it, and here it was, sitting on a park bench wearing a gray hoodie.

She spent the next several minutes watching him the way you watch a tennis match. When she crossed her ankles, did he? When she pushed her hair back, was there a hand through his own hair a few seconds later? Sometimes it seemed so and sometimes it did not, and she understood, with a small cold feeling, that she could not tell the difference between a person naturally matching her and a person doing it on purpose, which was the whole point, because according to the study nobody could. Then a second thought arrived, less cold: if she could not tell, then the information was useless as evidence, which meant she had to decide about him some other way, the way people had decided about people for all the centuries before 1999.

Also, and this was the part she felt culpability about even though no one had assigned it, she had changed her own posture twice to test him. She had uncrossed her ankles and waited. Whatever he did next, she had contaminated it, and she could not say whether that was a small dishonesty or just the ordinary way people leaned toward each other without planning to.

A jogger went past, then two little kids chasing a pigeon that was clearly going to win. The boy asked her what she was thinking, and she considered lying, and then did not.

"I read about this study once," she said. "1999. These researchers, Chartrand and Bargh. People liked a conversation partner more when the partner copied their posture and gestures, and they didn't even notice the copying. And you and I were sitting the same way, elbows and everything, and I couldn't stop checking."

He looked at his own elbows as though meeting them for the first time. Then he laughed, not the polite kind. "I wasn't doing it on purpose," he said. "But I can't prove that either. That's kind of the problem, right?"

"It's exactly the problem," Florence said.

"Okay," he said, and deliberately put both hands in his pockets, ruining the symmetry entirely, and looked at her. "So we'll have to go by something else."

She picked up the soda can, still cold, and clinked it against his.

activity: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
knowledge_domain: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
fact: Kiddush is a blessing recited over wine or grape juice to begin Sabbath and Jewish festival meals, marking the day as holy.
story:
Lea practiced in the back seat the whole way to her grandmother's house, her lips moving against the window glass while her mother navigated the highway. The words were in Hebrew, then Hebrew she could understand only in pieces, and she had written them out phonetically on an index card that she now held below the window line so her mother wouldn't see. Her grandmother had asked her, on the phone Tuesday, in a voice that pretended to be casual. This year, would Lea like to make Kiddush? Not just say the blessing, but lead the whole meal, start to finish.

"You're murmuring," her mother said at a red light. "Is something wrong?"

"I'm fine."

At the house, the smell hit her first: brisket, onions, something with cinnamon drying at the edges of a pan. Her grandmother's kitchen at holiday time had a way of circumscribing the whole world; nothing outside it, not the exam she'd failed, not the news, seemed able to get in. Her grandmother stood at the counter with wet hands and a dish towel over one shoulder, and behind her, already at the table, sat an assortment of uncles and cousins who had arrived early, the way they always did, to argue about parking.

"So," her grandmother said. "Ready?"

Lea set the index card on the counter, face down. "I've been practicing. I can do the words."

"The words are the smallest part." Her grandmother dried her hands slowly, folding the towel into a neat rectangle. "You have to know when to start. You have to see the table, see who's waiting, see who's hungry and who will wait all night for you if you let them. Your grandfather did it by watching, not by reading."

There was the problem, then, laid out plainly between the brisket and the wine. Lea had learned the blessing the way she learned everything, alone, in the car, phonetics and repetition, the method that had gotten her through every exam. But her grandmother was describing something else, a kind of attention, and Lea didn't know if it could be practiced in a Toyota.

She went out to the porch to call Louis, who had answered on the second ring with the sound of his siblings behind him. He'd grown up doing this, all of it, every Friday night.

"Everyone says the same thing," Louis told her. "It's not a performance. Nobody's grading you. My dad mixes up the words half the time and everyone just says amen anyway."

"That's not comforting. That's terrifying. If nobody's grading, then nobody can tell me if I did it right."

"Right according to who, though?" She could hear him shift, the noise behind him dimming as he closed a door. "Kiddush isn't a test. It's the blessing over the wine that starts the meal, the thing that makes the day holy instead of just dinner. If you say it and everyone drinks, it worked. That's the whole rubric."

Lea turned the index card over in her hands, phone tucked against her shoulder. Two ways of thinking stood in front of her like two doors: the version where she recited flawlessly and the table judged her, and the version Louis described, where the words were less a password than an opening, a thing that let the evening begin. She suspected the truth was somewhere awkwardly between, and that she would have to find the exact spot herself, out loud, in front of twenty relatives.

Inside, the table was being set around her. Her grandmother poured the wine without being asked, a small glass for Lea, left at her place, and it caught the overhead light in a way that made the liquid seem briefly evanescent, there and trembling and easily spilled. An uncle called out that they were starving. A younger cousin drummed her fork.

"You don't have to," her grandmother said quietly, passing behind her. "Under no kind of duress, you understand. I asked because I thought you'd want it. Not because anyone needs you to be perfect."

Lea picked up the glass. The card stayed on the counter, face down, and she felt its absence like a missing tooth. She stood, and the table quieted in stages, forks settling, chairs creaking, her youngest cousin shushed by her mother mid-sentence.

Lea lifted the cup a little higher than she meant to, and began.

activity: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
knowledge_domain: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
fact: The limiting reactant is the one that runs out first, and it sets the greatest amount of product a reaction can make.
story:
The chalk dust had habituated Ms. Krause to washing her hands twice a period, but nothing had habituated Camille to the smell of the chemistry room by the third week, that sharp ghost of sulfur that clung to sleeves and followed her into the hallway. She sat in the second row with her notebook open to a problem she had copied three times, and it still refused to mean anything. 14.2 grams of nitrogen gas reacts with hydrogen gas to form ammonia, the problem said, and the question was how many moles of ammonia could form. She knew the molar mass of nitrogen was 28.02 grams per mole. She knew a mole was 6.02 times ten to the twenty-third of anything. She knew, in the way you know the capital of a country you have never visited, that the answer was out there.

The problem was that she could not get from grams to moles to anything else without losing her way in the middle, and the quiz on Friday would not wait for her to find it.

At lunch she took her tray to the corner table where Cecilia was already making sandwiches out of what the cafeteria line had given her. Cecilia did this most days, assembling rather than eating, two slices of bread, a pile of turkey, a lake of mustard. Today she had a different arrangement: one heel of bread, an entire untouched sandwich's worth of turkey, and three cheese slices still in their plastic.

"You have so much turkey," Camille said, dropping her bag on the bench.

"And one piece of bread." Cecilia held it up. "So I can make exactly half a sandwich. Maybe less."

"That's depressing."

"That's lunch." Cecilia began folding turkey into the bread until the single slice bulged and could not close. "There's a whole second sandwich in here, just sitting around, useless, because the bread ran out."

Camille stopped with her own tray halfway to the table. She had been carrying the problem in her head since second period, the way you carry a song you can only hum, and something about the folded bread and the stranded turkey made the two things touch. "The bread sets it," she said slowly. "How many sandwiches you can actually make. Not the turkey. The turkey could make more, but it can't, because there isn't enough bread."

"Sure," said Cecilia, mouth full. "Why are you looking at me like that?"

"Because I think you just fixed my chemistry grade." Camille sat down and pulled out the notebook, flattening it between the milk carton and the tray. She wrote it small, in the margin where nobody would see it: bread = the reactant that runs out first. It decides everything. The turkey is just extra.

Reese slid into the seat across from her, saw the notebook open at lunch, and groaned. "You're doing stoichiometry at the table now."

"It's not stoichiometry, it's sandwiches." Camille turned the notebook so Reese could see the margin. "If you have a ton of turkey and almost no bread, the bread is the one that runs out first, and it sets the greatest amount of sandwich you can make. That's the whole thing."

Reese looked at the margin, then at Cecilia's plate, where the evidence was still visible, the exhausted slice and the surplus of turkey beside it. "Ms. Krause called that the limiting reactant on Monday," Reese said. "I wrote it down and then forgot it."

"The limiting reactant," Camille repeated, and the word settled into place like a key finding its lock. "Okay. Okay, so." She flipped back to the problem and worked fast, dividing 14.2 by 28.02, and then the next step arrived before she had to hunt for it, and the step after that, and she filled half the page before the bell logic caught up with her. "Wait. The problem gave me a mass of one reactant. How do I know if it's the limiting one?"

"You don't, yet," Reese said. "You'd need to know how much of the other one you have."

"Then how does anyone ever know they did it right?"

Reese shrugged and stole a cheese slice. Cecilia said, "You count your bread."

That afternoon, in the lab room that still smelled faintly of Friday's burnt peanut, Camille asked Ms. Krause only one question, whether a problem could give you both amounts and make you decide which one ran out first, and Ms. Krause said yes, that it was half the work, and moved on to weigh out white powder for the next class. Camille wrote the answer in her notebook and underlined nothing. She was aware, with a clarity that was almost uncomfortable, that she could still get Friday's quiz wrong, that the bread might run out in her head somewhere between the second and third step, that understanding a thing at lunch was not the same as holding onto it under a ticking clock.

She stayed anyway, after the last bell, and did three more problems at the counter by the window. The third one she checked twice, because she was not certain, and she wrote "not certain" beside it in small letters, and then she packed her bag and walked out through the emptying hallway with the notebook heavy against her back, its pages holding one thing she had and two things she still had to find.

Outside, Cecilia was waiting by the fence, eating what appeared to be turkey rolled around cheese, no bread at all. "Did it work?" Cecilia asked.

"Half a sandwich's worth," Camille said, and held up the notebook. "Ask me again tomorrow."

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: In a 1974 study by Donald Dutton and Arthur Aron, men who had just crossed a frightening suspension bridge were more likely to call a female interviewer afterward than men who crossed a sturdy bridge.
story:
Faith arrived at the counter eleven minutes early, which she decided to think of as five minutes early plus a margin for error. The ice cream shop smelled of waffle cones and hot fudge, and behind the glass the freezers hummed in a way that made the whole room feel air conditioned from the floor up. She had chosen a stool near the window where she could watch the door, and she rehearsed, once, the opening line she had settled on in the shower, something about how the shop's mint color had always struck her as a brave choice for a wall.

Giuliano came in shaking rain off his jacket, and the first thing he said was that the horror movie they had just left had enervated him completely, that he felt like a wrung towel, that his legs were still shaking on the walk over. Faith admitted hers were too. There had been a scene in the third act involving a hallway and a door that opened on its own, and the whole theater had flinched at once, a single organism, and now the two of them sat with the aftermath of it between them like a shared secret they hadn't chosen.

He ordered a triple scoop with three hot sauces, an arrangement the cashier raised an eyebrow at, and Faith, who had planned to be modest and dignified, heard herself order the same. "When in doubt, go epicurean," Giuliano said, gesturing at the mountain of whipped cream the cashier was adding. "My dad's word. He uses it for everything, even grilled cheese." Faith laughed, and noticed that her laugh came out louder than she expected, and that her heart, which had been pounding since the hallway scene, had not slowed down even now that the danger was fictional and two blocks behind them.

She turned her spoon in the melting mint and said, carefully, the thing she had been turning over since the lights came up. "In psychology, Ms. Bekele told us about this study. 1974, by Donald Dutton and Arthur Aron. Men who had just crossed a frightening suspension bridge were more likely to call a female interviewer afterward than men who crossed a sturdy bridge." Giuliano stopped mid-scoop. "Called her," he repeated. "As in asked her out?" Faith said that was the finding, exactly as it was printed in their textbook, and that Ms. Bekele had given them no more than that.

"So the scary bridge men thought they liked her," Giuliano said slowly, "and the sturdy bridge men just walked away thinking nothing." He scraped the bottom of his cup. "Which means, if we're being honest about tonight, that neither of us can trust a single thing we're feeling right now. We just spent two hours being terrified together. Our hearts are doing whatever hearts do." He said it lightly, but Faith understood that he was offering her an exit, a clean and scientific door out of the evening, and she sat with the spoon in her hand and considered whether to take it.

Her mother would have taken it. Her mother believed in waiting until you were calm to know your own mind, in sleeping on things, in the furlough she had once taken from a boyfriend in her twenties that had turned permanent without anyone announcing it. But Nelson, who was Faith's friend the way a lit match is a friend to a fuse, believed the opposite: that the pounding heart was the truth and everything afterward was the excuse. Faith had listened to both of them across two lunches and one late phone call, and neither position had won. What she had instead was a suspicion that they were both describing parts of the same evening, the way the two scoops in her bowl were both ice cream and still not the same flavor.

"Here's what I actually think," she said. "I was scared before you sat down, and I'm not scared now, and my heart is still going. That's not proof of anything. It's just a thing that's true." Giuliano considered this with the seriousness of a boy who had built a sundae like a cathedral. "So you're saying we can't know," he said. "I'm saying we can't know yet," Faith said. "The study doesn't say the bridge men were wrong. It just says they called. Nobody followed up on what happened after." Giuliano set down his spoon. "You're telling me the textbook ends before the good part."

Outside, the rain had thinned to something more like a suggestion, and the window fogged and cleared with the breath of the shop. Faith looked at the last of the mint, then at him, then at the small stack of napkins between them, which someone had folded into a neat and unnecessary triangle. "There's a bench under the awning two doors down," she said. "Sturdy, no suspension, nothing frightening about it." Giuliano took his jacket off the back of the stool. "Then let's go sit there," he said, "and see what happens to our pulses."

activity: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
knowledge_domain: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
fact: Hormonal IUDs and contraceptive implants fail in fewer than 1 in 100 users a year, because once placed by a clinician they do not depend on daily use.
story:
Gavin locked the stall door in the third-floor bathroom and took out the folded pages of his notes. In twenty minutes he was supposed to stand in front of Ms. Ramírez's ninth-grade health class and explain consent, contraception, and how to get tested at the clinic on Marsh Street, because Ms. Ramírez had decided that a peer educator would say things a sixteen-year-old would actually hear. He had volunteered in a moment of certainty that now felt like it had belonged to someone else. He read the first line under his breath, then out loud, and the sound of his own voice in the tiled room was so strange that he stopped.

He had never thought about how much work it was to say a true thing carefully. Consent, he had written, is ongoing and can be withdrawn, which was correct and also sounded like a legal document. He tried again. "If someone says yes once, that yes doesn't cover forever," he said to the stall door, and that was better, that was something a fourteen-year-old might actually carry home. He wondered whether clarity was a kind of enfranchisement, whether giving someone the words gave them the power to use them, and then he wondered if that was too fancy an idea to say out loud in front of thirty kids who would laugh at anything that smelled of effort.

The reason he knew the contraception numbers at all was Noemie. Two weeks ago she had asked him to come with her to the Marsh Street clinic, not because she needed company exactly, she said, but because she wanted a witness, someone who would remember the appointment the same way she remembered it. In the little room with the paper-covered table, the nurse had laid out the options like a dealer laying out cards. Noemie had done the math on the pill, four hundred and fifty chances a year to forget, and the nurse had nodded and said that was exactly the problem. Then she had said the thing Gavin had written down in his smallest handwriting: hormonal IUDs and implants fail in fewer than 1 in 100 users a year, because once placed by a clinician they don't depend on daily use. Noemie had looked at Gavin across the room, eyebrows up, as if to say, why does anyone ever start with the pill, and the nurse had laughed and said people like choices, and some people don't want anything placed.

Gavin leaned against the stall wall now and tried to reconstruct the rest. The clinic took walk-ins on Tuesdays and Thursdays. Testing was free for anyone under nineteen. You didn't need a parent, though the nurse had said, quietly, that telling a trusted adult was usually easier than not telling one. He ran through it, testing each fact the way you'd test a knot. Somewhere in the middle he lost the thread and stood there in the fluorescent hush, and the question came to him gently, the way questions did when he let them: was he actually going to be able to answer whatever they asked, or only deliver what he'd rehearsed?

The door swung open and someone came in. Water, the hand dryer's interminable roar, then Rian's voice saying, "Gavin? You're hiding in here, aren't you." Gavin flushed, unlocked the stall, and found Rian leaning against the sinks with the particular slouch of someone who had been sent to find him.

"I'm not hiding. I'm practicing my elocution," Gavin said, and regretted it immediately, but Rian only grinned.

"Your what?"

"How you say a thing. The delivery." Gavin spread the folded pages on the sink counter, where a thin thread of water immediately darkened one corner. Rian glanced at the headings and didn't grin anymore.

"I didn't know any of that stuff last year," Rian said. "I mean actually know it. There were rumors and there was the internet, and neither one was, like, reliable." He tapped the page near the bottom. "The one in a hundred thing. Is that real?"

"I was there when the nurse said it. Noemie was comparing options and the nurse walked her through why the long-acting ones work better in practice." Gavin heard himself say it plainly and felt something settle, the fact holding its shape in his mouth. "They don't depend on you remembering anything."

Rian was quiet for a second, watching the tap drip. "So when you're up there, what if someone asks something you don't know?"

"Then I say I don't know and I find out and I tell them after." Gavin folded the pages along their wet crease. "That's the honest version. The rest is just saying true things slowly enough for people to catch them."

The bell for the period change rang through the wall. Rian pushed off the sink and held the door, and Gavin walked out with his notes still damp at one corner, reading the first line again as they went.

"Start with the part about saying yes once," Rian said. "That's the part nobody ever tells you."
